He shook his head slowly, but his chin lifted as he did it, and his eyes caught the pale light and held it, bright and wet and wide open.

His foot tapped once against the cobblestone. Then again.

"Nothing to be done, I suppose." He finally met Aldric's eyes, and his voice was quiet, almost tender with regret. "Nothing at all to be done."

The 7:42 ran the same route it had for eleven years, and Petra had memorized every lurch and sway of it. She sat in the third seat from the back—always the third—her canvas bag on her lap, fingers laced through the strap.

Marcus slid into the seat beside her. She hadn't seen him in eight months.

Nothing about him had changed. That was the first thing she checked.

"You're still taking this bus," he said, not unkindly.

"Someone has to." She shifted her bag an inch to the left, then an inch back. "You look the same."

"You say that like it's a compliment."

"It is."

He glanced at the window, at the city streaming past. "I heard you turned down the job. The one in the new district."

Petra's jaw tightened. "Too far from everything." She pressed her thumbnail into the canvas strap, a slow, deliberate crescent. "You know how I get in open spaces. All that glass and sky. Those new towers with the lobbies that go up forever." She shook her head. "I can't work somewhere I feel exposed like that."

"The commute would've been fine. Same number of stops."

"It's not about stops, Marcus."

He nodded slowly. Outside, the bus rolled past the corner where the old laundromat used to be. A smoothie franchise had taken its place three months ago, bright green signage where the handwritten hours had been. Petra's eyes moved to it and stayed there a half-second too long. Her shoulders climbed toward her ears. She pulled them down deliberately, the way you correct posture you've been correcting your whole life.

"I just do better in contained spaces," she said. "Somewhere with walls I can account for."

"You used to say that about us."

She didn't answer. She was looking at the seat in front of her, which had a new fabric pattern—blue diamonds instead of the grey stripes she'd spent years not-quite-looking-at. Her thumb moved faster against the strap. She hadn't noticed it until now and now she couldn't stop noticing it.

"They reupholstered," she said.

"What?"

"The seats." Her voice was very even. "They reupholstered."

Marcus looked at her the way he used to, like he was reading a map in a language he mostly knew. "Petra."

"I'm fine." She smoothed her hand across the blue diamonds once, twice. "I just don't like not knowing what I'm walking into. Big open plazas, crowds that shift around you—you lose your bearings." She said it firmly, like a diagnosis she'd already made peace with. "That's all it is."

The bus groaned around a familiar corner. Third seat from the back. Same time. Same route.

The seats were wrong and Marcus was here and somewhere in her chest, a door she'd locked from the inside was rattling on its hinges.

"Same time tomorrow?" he asked, standing for his stop.

She looked straight ahead. "I'll be here."

Gerald watched her. She was standing at a slight angle to him—not quite facing him, not quite facing the door—the way a person stands when they want two exits available.

"I haven't started on him yet," Gerald said carefully. "He's still in cold storage."

She nodded, and something moved through her face—a tightening around the eyes, a brief stillness—before she covered it with another small smile. Her hand found her coat lapel again. "Of course. "It's fine."

"I worry I made it weird." She glanced at the curtain. "Is someone else here?"

"No," he said.

She held his eyes for exactly one beat, then looked away first, toward the fox on the shelf. Her shoulders dropped a quarter inch. "Sorry. I just thought I heard—" She shook her head. "Forget it. I'm sorry for taking up your afternoon. Really. You can call me whenever he's ready. Or don't, even. I can check back."

"I'll call you," Gerald said.

"You don't have to."

"I know."

She buttoned the top button of her coat, even though it wasn't cold. On her way to the door she passed the curtained doorway and her stride changed—just slightly, just for one step—before she caught herself and walked out into the gray afternoon.

"Look at them," Dex said, without turning around. He had a program rolled tight in his fist. "Twenty-two, maybe. Twenty-three. You know what I could do at twenty-three?"

"Write sentences that needed less work," Marguerite said, settling beside him on the bleacher.

He laughed, but his eyes didn't move from the girls in silver. "The new draft," he said. "The publisher wants it younger. Fresher voice, they said. You know what that means."

"It means they want it to sell."

"It means they think I'm done." He finally looked at her, and the lines around his eyes seemed deeper under the circus lights. "Fifty-six isn't done, Marguerite. Doctorow was writing masterworks at seventy. Updike. You tell them that."

"I'll tell them."

But even as she spoke, she was aware that her shoulder was touching his—that she'd angled herself toward him when she sat down, closed the gap between them to almost nothing. Around them the bleachers were filling, families pressing into rows, children climbing over knees, and Marguerite found herself tracking the crowd the way she tracked a room at parties: cataloguing the clusters, the pairs, the groups of four. The usher at the far entrance had a hand on someone's arm, guiding them. A man two rows down had his arm around a woman, and Marguerite watched that arm longer than she needed to.

"The thing about getting old," Dex continued, "is that nobody tells you it happens to your reputation first. The body's fine. The mind's fine. But suddenly you're a *legacy* writer, which is just a polite way of saying—"

"Dex."

"—a polite way of saying you're furniture."

The acrobats dropped and were caught. The crowd exhaled as one, a single warm sound, and Marguerite felt it move through her like something she was hungry for. She pressed her knee against Dex's without deciding to. He didn't seem to notice.

"They'll drop me eventually," he said. "Everyone gets dropped. You know what the shelf life is for a man my age who isn't writing thrillers?"

"I'm not dropping you."

He waved this away. "You're contractually obligated not to."

"No," she said. "I'm not."

He looked at her then—really looked—and Marguerite realized she'd said it too plainly, too quickly. She looked back up at the acrobats. The silver girls were taking their bow, and the crowd around her was cheering, everyone leaning into everyone else, and she clapped hard, harder than the act required, her palms stinging in the cold air.

"You just don't want to lose the commission," Dex said, smiling.

"Obviously," she said.

The next act came on. Dex went back to worrying aloud about relevance and legacy and the cruelty of an industry that worshipped youth. Marguerite listened, and nodded, and did not move her knee away from his.

Maya sat with her hands folded in her lap, though her fingers kept finding each other, interlacing and pulling apart the way children worry a loose thread. She had positioned her chair so she could see both the office door and the window that faced the parking lot. She hadn't done it consciously. She never did.

"I just don't want to become someone who does this to other people," she said. Her voice was steady, practiced. "That's what keeps me up at night. My mother never left my father, and her mother never left hers. I see the pattern. I understand it academically. But what if I'm already inside it and I can't tell?" She laughed once, short and dry. "What if I'm already him?"

Dr. Reeves wrote something. Maya's eyes moved briefly to the window. A car had slowed on the street below. It didn't stop. Her shoulders dropped half an inch.

"My sister stopped returning my calls," Maya continued, leaning forward now, elbows on her knees, speaking with the focused urgency of someone making a case. "What if I pushed her away because some part of me operates the same way he does? What if I'm doing it without knowing?" She pressed two fingers against her sternum absently, as though checking for a heartbeat she wasn't sure was there.

The office door opened—just the receptionist, placing a water glass on the table outside. Maya's whole body turned toward the sound before her mind caught up. For one suspended second her face was open and raw, the face of someone expecting to find a room empty, a person gone, a hand that had let go. Then she registered the receptionist, and the expression closed like a shutter.

"Sorry," she said, to no one in particular.

"You were saying—about your sister," Dr. Reeves prompted gently.

Maya nodded and looked back at her hands. "Right. Yes. I need to understand where I learned this, so I don't pass it on." She said it cleanly, with conviction. Beneath the chair, her foot had found the leg of Dr. Reeves's desk and pressed lightly against it, the way a child presses against something solid in the dark.

1190.scenario:
The research station's screened porch offered a thin boundary between the humid press of the jungle and the relative cool inside. Principal Marta Voss stood at the railing, watching the younger teachers set up the student camp below, her arms crossed tight over her chest.

"You need to be careful with the local guides," she called down to Daniel, the newest hire. "They'll offer to carry everything, and next thing you know they're charging the school for services nobody approved." She tapped the railing with one finger. "I've seen it happen. Always read what you're signing."

Daniel nodded patiently. He'd heard some version of this four times since they'd landed.

Marta turned back toward the porch mirror—a small square thing someone had nailed up for practical reasons—and her gaze snagged on her own reflection before she could stop it. She looked away quickly, the way you'd look away from a bright light. She moved to the far end of the railing instead, busying her hands with a knot in the mosquito netting.

"And the supply vendors in the village," she continued, voice steady, authoritative, "they quote one price and invoice another. You have to watch the line items."

Below, a burst of laughter from the younger teachers. They were hoisting a tent pole together, their arms easy and loose. Marta's hand went briefly to the soft underside of her jaw—a quick, unconscious press of fingers—before she pulled it back and gripped the railing again.

She noticed a new spider plant someone had hung from the porch beam, green and extravagant and bursting with runners.

She did not look at it long.

"Just—make sure you're documenting everything," she said, her voice carrying the familiar authority. "Nobody's going to protect the school's interests but us."

The jungle breathed its thick green breath around her. Somewhere in the canopy, a bird she couldn't name called out, urgent and high, and Marta Voss straightened her spine and kept her eyes on the work below.

1184.scenario:
The common room smelled like burnt coffee and old vinyl. Maya had been sitting with her back to the wall for forty minutes, watching Declan fold and refold the same dish towel while he talked.

"It's the county fair thing," she said, pulling her knees up onto the couch cushion. "All those people packed in. The midway alone—" She shook her head. "I looked at the map online and there's basically one exit on the south end. One. If something happened, everyone would just—"

"Nothing's going to happen." Declan set the dish towel down, then immediately picked it back up.

"You don't know that. Open spaces like that, you're completely exposed." She gestured broadly. "At least in here I can see all four walls."

Declan laughed, soft and careful. He crossed the room and sat beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. Maya kept talking about crowd density, about the parking situation, about how she'd read that panic could move through a crowd like a current—but her right hand, which had been resting near his thigh, drew back into her lap the moment he settled beside her.

"So just skip it," he said.

"I might." She was looking at the window now, not at him. "Unless—" She stopped.

"Unless?"

She turned, finally meeting his eyes, and something moved across her face—quick and involuntary, the way a hand jerks from a hot pan. Not dread exactly. More like recognition. She looked away again before he could read it fully.

"Unless I can find parking close to the exit," she finished.

Declan nodded slowly. He reached over and tucked a strand of hair behind her ear, a small thing, almost nothing. Maya smiled—genuinely—but her shoulders rose a half-inch toward her ears and stayed there, a body bracing for something it couldn't name.

"I'll drive," he said.

"Yeah." She exhaled. "Yeah, okay. That helps. The crowd thing is just—it's a lot, you know? All that open sky and nowhere to—"

He took her hand. Just held it, loosely, in his.

She kept talking about the fair.

Her thumb moved once against his knuckles, almost imperceptibly, like a question she wasn't ready to ask out loud.

1187.scenario:
The laminated menu stuck to Dara's fingers. She set it down without reading it, then picked it up again.

"You know they found another body on Route 9," she said, studying the list of breakfast specials without really seeing them. "Third one this year. That's what I'm saying—it's not safe, driving at night anymore." She glanced toward the window, then quickly back down. "People don't take it seriously enough. One wrong exit and that's it. Gone."

Across the booth, Marcus stirred his coffee.

Dara's eyes moved to the trucker two tables over, who was laughing loudly with the waitress. Her shoulders pulled inward, almost imperceptibly. She watched them for a moment—the ease of it, the way the woman touched the man's arm without thinking—then redirected her gaze to the salt shaker.

"I told my sister the same thing," she continued. "Just—statistically. The odds aren't good for people who aren't paying attention." Her fingers found the paper placemat and began folding the corner back and forth. Fold, unfold. Fold, unfold. "You can't just trust that everything will be fine."

Marcus looked up. "You want to order?"

The waitress was already approaching. Dara opened her mouth, then closed it. She looked down at the menu she hadn't read. Her jaw tightened slightly, the way it did before she said something she'd already decided not to say.

"Just coffee," she said, without looking up.

The waitress left. The trucker laughed again. Dara watched the window, where headlights swept past in the dark.

"People really do just disappear," she said quietly. "And nobody sees it coming."

Marcus said nothing. He'd learned, in eight months of this, that she wasn't really talking to him.

1193.scenario:
The passageway was narrow enough that Headmaster Crane had to turn sideways at the bend, his lantern throwing amber shapes across the stone. Elliot followed three steps behind, close enough to seem compliant.

"You understand what's at stake," Crane said, not turning around. "If you take point on this investigation, every mistake lands on you. Every misstep. I've watched students volunteer for positions like this and come apart under the weight." He paused at a rusted iron door, running his thumb along the handle without opening it. "Leadership is a particular kind of loneliness. I want you to be certain before you agree to anything."

Elliot nodded, though Crane couldn't see it.

What Elliot noticed, without meaning to, was the sound coming from somewhere above them—the muffled percussion of the dining hall, chairs scraping, voices layered into a single warm noise. His body oriented toward it the way a compass needle finds north. He caught himself listening for specific laughs, specific names, wondering whether the table by the east window was full yet and whether anyone had noticed he wasn't there.

"Sir," he said, "I just don't want to make a decision that puts everyone else in danger."

Crane finally turned, studying him. Elliot held the headmaster's gaze steadily, arms loose at his sides. But one hand had found the wall, fingertips pressed flat against the cold stone—as though measuring the distance back to the door, back to the corridor, back to wherever the others were eating dinner without him.

The 6:42 to Portland was already boarding when Mara spotted Daniel on the platform. She told herself she wouldn't cross the yellow line. She told herself she would simply wait.

She waited for eleven seconds before walking over.

"I just don't want people to think I was the one who—" she started, before he'd even fully turned around. "I mean, you know how mutual friends are. They pick a side. They make it into a whole *narrative*, and I can't stand the idea of everyone thinking I'm the villain in whatever story you've been telling."

Daniel looked tired. "I haven't been telling any story, Mara."

"Because Priya already gave me this *look* at Jonah's thing last month, and I—" Her hand moved toward his arm, then pulled back. She tucked it into her jacket pocket instead. "I just need people to understand what actually happened."

"What did happen?" he asked, quietly.

Her mouth opened. The train doors hissed. Somewhere behind her a child was crying, and she focused on that sound with sudden, grateful intensity—turned her head toward it, let her eyes track the source, bought herself four full seconds of not having to look at his face.

"I don't want Priya thinking I'm the kind of person who—"

"Mara."

She was already stepping back. One foot, then the other, redistributing her weight toward the exit, toward the parking structure, toward anywhere that was not this exact spot on this exact platform with this exact man who was watching her with an expression she couldn't decode and therefore couldn't survive.

"I just wanted to clear the air," she said. "For everyone else's sake."

Daniel nodded slowly. He didn't try to stop her.

She was three benches away before she exhaled.

1200.scenario:
The yacht rocked gently in the harbor, and Marcus kept one hand on the brass railing the entire time—not because the water was rough. It was glassy, almost motionless. He kept his hand there anyway, fingers white around the metal, as though the vessel might suddenly decide to go somewhere without his permission.

"The Hendricks portfolio," he said, watching Diane arrange documents across the teak table. She moved them into a configuration he didn't recognize, a layout he hadn't asked for, and his jaw tightened. "That's what I want to talk about. If the market corrects in Q3, I need to know we have a cushion. I've seen men lose everything, Diane. Everything. My father—" He stopped himself. "I need to know the money is safe."

Diane nodded, sliding a prospectus toward him. He didn't pick it up immediately. Instead, his eyes tracked the movement of a deckhand crossing the stern behind her—someone he hadn't briefed, someone whose job on this boat he hadn't confirmed. His gaze followed the man until he disappeared below deck, and only then did Marcus look down at the papers.

"A diversified bond ladder," Diane said, "gives you exactly the kind of cushion you're describing."

"What about liquidity?" Marcus asked. His voice was steady, even authoritative. His free hand, the one not gripping the railing, moved to the armrest of his chair and pressed flat against it, as if taking a reading of the deck's intentions. The boat shifted a half-inch in its mooring. His shoulders rose toward his ears before he pulled them back down, smoothing his jacket with deliberate calm.

"Fully liquid within seventy-two hours," she said.

"Good." He nodded. "Good." But his eyes had already moved to the helm, unmanned now, the wheel resting at a slight angle nobody had set. He stared at it for a beat too long.

"Marcus?"

"Sorry." He turned back to her. "I want to see all the projections. Every scenario. I don't like surprises." He said it the way a man says *I don't like olives*—casually, as a preference. But his hand found the railing again.

Maren set the crayon drawings on the activity table, smoothing them flat with her palms. Her granddaughter Lily, six years old and already proud of her work, climbed into the chair across from her and waited.

"They're good," Maren said, studying the purple horses and lopsided suns. "But good isn't what you want to be, sweetheart. Good is forgettable. Good is everyone." She tapped the page. "You want to be *remarkable*. You want people to remember your name."

Lily's lower lip shifted.

"I'm not trying to discourage you. I'm trying to save you from settling." Maren's voice was measured, practiced. "The worst thing in the world is to look back at your life and realize you coasted. That you had something real inside you and you let it go soft."

But when the child's hand reached across the table toward her arm—small fingers, innocent, seeking—Maren's whole body registered it before her mind could. She drew back an inch, just one, the way a person leans from heat. Her jaw tightened. She let the touch happen but her eyes went briefly to the door, cataloguing the distance, the same quiet arithmetic she had performed her entire life.

"Your mother was talented too," she continued, smoothing her sleeve. "She just never pushed herself." She glanced at the hallway again—the old reflex, the old geometry of exits. "Promise me you'll push yourself."

Lily nodded, not fully understanding.

Maren folded her hands on the table. Still. Deliberate. The way you hold something down.

1208.scenario:
The wind came in low and mean across the flats, and Detective Reyes kept her back to it, scanning the tree line the way she'd been scanning it since they'd arrived—a slow, methodical sweep, then back to the parking area, then to the road, then the tree line again. She wasn't aware she was doing it.

"You know what I told Hargrove?" she said, pulling her coat tighter without looking at Mikkelsen. "I told him this case needed somebody who actually gives a damn about the outcome. Half the people in that building are just—" she exhaled, a white cloud taken immediately by the wind— "just *filling seats*. Collecting a check. I've seen the reports they file. No follow-through. No hunger." She shook her head. "That's not me. That will never be me."

Mikkelsen hugged himself and said nothing. He was used to her speeches.

Her phone buzzed. She looked at it—her sister's name on the screen—and something happened to her face before she could stop it. A brief collapse, like a wall taking a hit. She silenced it and put the phone away, and her hand came back trembling slightly, though the temperature had not changed.

"Where was I," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Hargrove," Mikkelsen offered.

"Right." She turned back to the tree line. The sweep again—slow, automatic, hungry for movement. Her jaw was tight in a way that had nothing to do with the cold. "The problem with this department is nobody wants to be *great* anymore. They just want to be good enough." She laughed, short and humorless. "Good enough. Can you imagine?"

Her eyes went to the road. Then the parking area. Then the tree line.

Her sister hadn't called in eleven days, and the doctors had used the word *stable* the way people use it when they mean *for now*.

"You're not even listening," she said.

"I am," said Mikkelsen.

She nodded once, jaw still tight, still watching the tree line for something she couldn't name and wouldn't say.

1212.scenario:
The break room smelled of burnt coffee and someone's reheated fish. Priya set her lunch container on the table and watched Marcus arrange napkins beside his plate—a ritual she'd come to recognize as his way of settling himself before a conversation he'd already rehearsed.

"My grandmother made this recipe," he said, lifting the lid from his container. Steam curled up between them. "Forty years she made it. My mother made it. Now my kids want drive-through every night." He shook his head slowly. "You lose the food, you lose the story behind the food. You lose the story, and then what? What holds everything together?"

Priya nodded, spooning rice. She'd heard variations of this before—the language slipping from the grandchildren, the holidays shrinking, the old songs nobody bothered to learn. She understood it.

"Someone has to fight to keep it alive," Marcus continued. "Otherwise it just—" he snapped his fingers, "—gone."

The break room door swung open.

Three other staff members filed in, already mid-conversation, laughing about something from the morning shift. They glanced toward the corner table, and one of them—Darnell—said, "Oh good, Marcus is here. We were just saying we need someone to organize the holiday schedule rotation. You always know how to sort these things out."

Marcus's fork stopped moving.

His shoulders drew inward, almost imperceptibly, as though something had blown cold air across the back of his neck. His eyes dropped to his plate and made a small, quick circuit—container, napkins, table edge—the way a person checks exits. When he looked up, there was a half-second delay, a slight tightening around his jaw, before his expression arranged itself into something neutral.

"I'm sure anyone could handle it," he said, his voice carefully level. "Doesn't have to be me."

"Come on, you're good at it," Darnell pressed.

Marcus laughed—a short, dry sound that didn't involve his eyes. His free hand had moved under the table. Priya noticed, because she always noticed things, that he was pressing his thumb hard into his opposite palm.

"What I'm good at," he said, redirecting smoothly, the way water redirects around stone, "is making sure my kids know their grandfather's name and what village he came from. Everything else—" he gestured vaguely toward Darnell, toward the schedule, toward the whole proposition, "—somebody else can carry that."

The trail narrowed between two mossy boulders, and Marcus stopped walking.

"These roots will absolutely destroy your ankles," he said, pointing his walking stick at the gnarled wood threading across the path. He didn't look at the roots. His eyes moved left, then right, tracking the tree line where the afternoon light had begun to thin. "I've seen people twist them badly out here. Snap. Just like that. You'd be hobbling for weeks."

Priya stepped carefully over the roots and waited for him on the other side.

Marcus didn't follow. He stood at the gap between the boulders—a natural doorway, open on both sides—and his breathing had gone shallow without him seeming to notice. His head turned toward a sound in the brush. A bird, probably. His grip on the walking stick had whitened his knuckles.

"The rocks are slippery too," he continued, his voice still even, almost professorial. "Wet moss on granite is basically ice. Broken wrists, broken tailbones. I want you to be careful about every step."

He finally moved through the gap, but he positioned himself so his back was against the boulder as he passed it, his eyes never settling, cataloguing each shadow between the trees. Once through, he exhaled slowly—a breath he hadn't known he was holding.

"Anyway." He rolled his shoulder as if shaking something off. "Just watch where you put your feet."

Priya nodded, studying him.

He was already scanning again.

The late afternoon sun stretched their shadows long across the pasture as Delia walked the fence line with her protégé, Marcus. He'd been asking about expanding the herd—bringing in outside investors, splitting the operation.

"You need to be careful who you let in," Delia said, her voice carrying the flat certainty of someone who'd learned a lesson the hard way. "People smile at you, shake your hand, and the whole time they're counting what's yours." She pulled a loose staple from a post and turned it between her fingers. "I've seen good farmers sign papers they didn't understand and lose everything inside of three years. You let someone else's money touch your land, you'd better read every line twice."

Marcus nodded, watching her.

But Delia had gone quiet now, staring at the far end of the pasture where the old cattle barn still stood, its roof bowing gently in the middle. Her father had built it. Her grandfather had built the one before it. She pressed two fingers against her temple without seeming to notice she'd done it—the same place the headaches started, the ones that had begun arriving like her mother's had, right around this age, always on the left side. Her eyes moved slowly across the herd, pausing on the animals that walked with any stiffness, any irregularity, cataloguing them the way she'd begun cataloguing herself. She rolled her shoulder, testing something private.

"Anyway," she said, blinking back. "Never give anyone a stake they didn't earn."

Marcus studied her face. "You doing okay?"

"I'm fine," she said, already walking. "Just don't trust easy. That's all I'm telling you."

She didn't look back at the barn.

1215.scenario:
The leather chair creaked as Marcus settled into it, his hands folded in his lap with practiced stillness. Dr. Yuen waited, her pen hovering.

"I've been thinking a lot about my brother," Marcus began, his gaze drifting toward the window. "We used to talk every Sunday. Now it's been—" he counted silently, lips moving, "—eleven weeks. Eleven weeks, and I'm the one who keeps calling." He shook his head. "That's how it happens, isn't it? People just quietly stop showing up. You don't even notice until the silence is the loudest thing in the room."

Dr. Yuen nodded. "And that silence feels—"

"Unbearable." The word came out quickly, almost rehearsed. "I keep telling Diane we need to make more of an effort. With *everyone*. Friends, family. I told her last night, we can't just let people drift. Life gets too empty that way."

But as he said his wife's name, his right hand slid to his phone, which sat face-down on the armrest. He didn't look at it. He didn't need to—his thumb found it automatically, pressing the dark screen as though checking for warmth. His jaw tightened almost imperceptibly.

"She agrees with you?" Dr. Yuen asked.

"She says she does." Marcus smiled, a clean, convincing smile that didn't quite reach the small muscle flickering beneath his left eye. "She's been—busy lately. New project at work. Late nights." He exhaled slowly, the kind of exhale that is really an inhale in disguise. "Anyway. The point is, nobody should have to beg for connection. That's all I'm saying. Nobody should have to wonder if the people they love are still *there*."

He glanced at the door—not the way a person checks a door, but the way a person checks an *exit*. Then, almost immediately, he checked his phone again. Still dark. Still silent.

"I just don't want to end up alone," he said.

He was looking at Dr. Yuen when he said it. His thumb was pressing the phone so hard his knuckle had gone white.

1185.scenario:
The bell above the door had barely stopped ringing when Maren began.

"Nobody at the guild drinks nettle tea anymore," she said, lifting a bundle of dried herbs from the shelf and turning it over in her hands. "They all use the pre-packaged tinctures from the southern traders. I look like some kind of relic when I pull out my own blends." She set the bundle down and picked up another. "You should really start stocking the fashionable things, Petra. Something that signals you know what's current."

Petra glanced up from her mortar. "You came across town to tell me my shop is unfashionable?"

"I'm saying you might lose customers." Maren drifted toward the window, still talking. "The younger apprentices especially. They want to feel like they belong to something modern."

But Petra had stopped listening to the words. She was watching her sister's hands.

Maren held each herb jar for only a moment before setting it back—not browsing, but checking, verifying, as though the label might have changed since she'd last looked. When Petra had reached for a new jar from the shelf above her, Maren's eyes had tracked the movement and stayed there, fixed on Petra's face, reading it. Not the jar. Petra's face.

"—and the apprentices won't say anything to your face, of course," Maren continued, "but you know how they talk—"

"Maren."

Maren stopped. Her shoulders drew up slightly.

"What happened?" Petra asked.

"Nothing happened. I'm just saying the guild has changed and—"

"You've touched every jar on that shelf twice." Petra kept her voice level. "You watched my face when I reached for the dried valerian like you were waiting for me to tell you it wasn't real." She set down her pestle. "Something happened and you're trying to figure out if I'll think you're telling the truth before you decide whether to say it."

The shop went quiet. Outside, a cart rattled past on the cobblestones.

Maren put down the jar she was holding. Her jaw was tight in the way it got when she was deciding something.

"There was a woman on the road," she finally said. "Three nights ago. She was—" She stopped. Swallowed. "I know what I saw."

Petra pulled a stool from behind the counter and set it near her sister without a word.

1207.scenario:
The mist from the falls settled on Renata's arms like a second skin, and she stood very still, watching the way the water hit the rocks below. She had chosen this spot deliberately—open sky, nothing closing in, the kind of place where you could always, always walk away.

"I'm just saying you probably think I made it up," she said, not looking at Marco. "That's what people do. They smile and nod and then they go home and they think, *she's dramatic.*"

Marco reached for her hand. She let him take it, but her fingers stayed loose, ready.

"I don't think that."

"You don't know yet." She laughed, short and flat. "Give it a minute. Give it until I've told you the whole thing and you'll get that look." She turned to demonstrate the look—patient, pitying—and her gaze moved past him automatically, mapping the trail back to the parking lot, the gap between two boulders she could fit through, the open ledge to her left.

"Renata."

"No, I've seen it. I've watched people decide I'm unreliable in real time." She pulled her jacket tighter across her chest, though the evening was warm. Her shoulders had been creeping toward her ears for the last ten minutes; she hadn't noticed until just now, how her whole torso had been slowly, methodically folding inward. She pressed her spine straight against the effort of it—deliberate, like unlocking something.

"You could just tell me," he said. "And then you'd know."

She exhaled through her nose. Her eyes went to the waterfall, then the sky, then the path. The path again.

"The thing is," she said, "even if you believe me—even if everyone believes me—it doesn't change what my body remembers. It doesn't unknow anything." She said it like a complaint about him, about skeptics, about the whole exhausting business of being taken seriously. But her hand had drifted to her own wrist, fingers wrapping around the pulse point, and she stood there holding herself like she was checking whether she could still feel her own edges.

The water kept falling.

"I just need you to not make that face," she said.

1217.scenario:
The ceiling fan chopped the humid air into slow, useless rotations while Marisol spread her canvases across the kitchen table. Her mother, Delia, stood in the doorway watching, arms loose at her sides—until her eyes drifted to the stack of unopened envelopes on the counter, the ones with the bank's logo in the corner. Her hand found the doorframe. Her fingers pressed white against the wood.

"You know what my problem is?" Marisol said, not looking up. She was squinting at a half-finished painting of the reef, dragging a dry brush across coral she couldn't seem to get right. "I keep letting people tell me I'm not good enough. The São Paulo gallery rejected me, fine. But I'm *telling* you, Mamá, I will get into the Biennale. I will. If I quit now I'll never know." She set the brush down and looked at her mother with something raw and certain in her face. "That's what scares me most. Not knowing."

Delia nodded slowly. She crossed to the refrigerator, opened it, closed it without taking anything. She moved to the window that faced the marina, where their rental cottage—their *only* rental cottage since the second one flooded—sat dark and unoccupied for the third week running. Her gaze tracked the tourists walking the dock below, counting without meaning to, the way a tongue finds a sore tooth.

"Of course you'll get in," she said. Her voice was steady, warm even.

But when Marisol slid a canvas aside and one of the bank envelopes fluttered to the floor, Delia's breath caught—a small, sharp sound, barely audible over the fan. She bent to pick it up before her daughter could reach it, and held it against her chest a half-second too long, as if its weight were something she needed to feel before she put it back.

"You have real talent," she continued, setting the envelope face-down on the counter. "Don't let anyone take that from you."

Marisol smiled and turned back to her reef. Delia watched her daughter's hands move with such easy confidence across the canvas, and felt a complicated tenderness she couldn't name—because she was proud, genuinely proud, and also because the fan overhead was loud enough to cover the sound of her doing the arithmetic in her head again, the same arithmetic she'd been doing since April.

1211.scenario:
The bailiff called the next case, and Renata smoothed her blazer for the fourth time in as many minutes. She had rehearsed this custody argument for eleven weeks. Eleven weeks of annotated case law stacked on her kitchen table, of moot sessions with her paralegal, of lying awake running counterarguments until her ceiling became a whiteboard. She knew the brief cold.

She sat down at the plaintiff's table and immediately knocked her legal pad to the floor. Her hands, retrieving it, were shaking.

"You okay?" Marcus whispered from the gallery behind her.

"I'm worried about Danny," she said, not quite turning around, her eyes already fixed on the judge's bench. "He's been coughing since Tuesday. His mother's not going to take him to the doctor—she never does. He could have pneumonia and just be sitting in that apartment—" She stopped herself. Pressed her lips together. "Kids die from things people ignore. He's eight."

The judge entered. Everyone rose. Renata rose half a second late, having already dropped her gaze to her opening notes, scanning the first paragraph as if she had never seen it before, as if the words might have rearranged themselves overnight.

"We shouldn't have taken on the northern families," she said to Dani, her voice flat and certain. "I told the coordinator last week—we don't have the infrastructure. Now we have forty more people depending on us for water allocation and we can't even get the truck moving." She crossed her arms, then uncrossed them. "If the filtration fails again, that's on us. You understand that? That falls on us."

A child nearby dropped a metal cup and the clang rang out sharp across the gravel. Mira's whole body lurched sideways before she caught herself, one hand shooting out to grip the tent pole. Her eyes went wide and then immediately narrow, scanning the perimeter fence, the tree line, the gap between the medical station and the storage containers. Her breathing had gone shallow and quick even as her face settled back into its administrative frown.

"We're already spread too thin," she continued, her voice steady, reasonable, the voice of someone making a budget argument. Her free hand moved to her sternum and pressed there, flat-palmed, as if checking that something was still beating. "We make promises we can't keep and people suffer for it. That's the problem. We overcommit."

Dani reached for her arm. "Mira—"

"I'm not panicking." She stepped back from the tent pole, smoothed her jacket, looked briefly at the sky the way a person looks at the sky when they are really looking at it and not thinking about anything abstract at all. "I just think we need clearer boundaries about what we take on. For everyone's sake."

The truck horn sounded from the road—just a signal that it was moving again—and Mira exhaled so completely that her shoulders dropped two full inches. She hadn't known, apparently, that she'd been holding them up.

"Let's move," Garrett said. "I will not be the reason we're late."

He said it to the trees. He said it to the record he'd never blemished. He kept his eyes on the path ahead and not on the boy's wrists, which bore the same kind of marks that Garrett had spent thirty years learning not to look at in mirrors.

She gave him nothing.

He looked back at the uniformed officers. One of them—young, maybe twenty-five—was running a thumb along the edge of his sidearm holster, easy and unconscious, the way you touched something familiar. It didn't.

"I need names," he said to Reyes. "Written. I need to know exactly who can connect a document back to me, because when this goes sideways—and it will go sideways—I need to know where it came from. I've seen what happens. I've *seen* it."

"You keep saying that."

A breath moved through her that was too careful, too managed, the kind you take when you are trying not to feel exactly what you're feeling.

"Anyway," she said, "the point is you can't count on the body. You can't make plans around it."

He was quiet. The motor home hummed.

She looked down at her open hands, then closed them again. Looked out the window. The road kept giving itself to them, mile after mile, more of it than they could use.

Her eyes moved without permission to Fletcher's face, reading it the way she'd learned to read rooms—exits, expressions, the slight compression around his mouth that might mean disappointment. There was nothing there. He was just listening. Still, her shoulders had drawn upward, almost to her ears, and she made herself lower them.

"Anyway," she said, louder than she meant to, "I'm just trying to protect you from the same mistake."

Fletcher nodded slowly. "I hear you."

She turned away, ostensibly to examine a stone angel in the corner, but really to give her hands somewhere to go. She straightened a dried flower arrangement that didn't need straightening. *What if it falls through?* she thought, and in her chest the sentence didn't attach itself to the deal.

It attached itself to Fletcher standing there, patient, still willing to walk into meetings at her side.

She turned back around, businesslike, briefcase in hand.

Renata's chin came up. Her eyes tracked the contact—hand on shoulder, hand dropping away—with the quiet efficiency of someone who had learned to read rooms before they could read books. She was watching his hands. She watched them constantly in conversations like this—where the hands went, whether they found the back pocket, the crossed-arm position, the small telltale drift toward a phone. His stayed still. She noted this and distrusted her own noting of it.

"The thing about big open spaces," she continued, louder than she needed to, "is that your brain loses its anchor points. There's no perimeter. You can't locate yourself relative to anything stable." She was pacing now, a tight oval between the counter and the table. "It's a legitimate neurological response. I've read about it."

"I know it is."

She glanced up. Her jaw tightened almost imperceptibly, a small brace against whatever came next. When nothing came—no *but*, no *however*, no patient exhale—she looked at him for a full two seconds, which for her was a long time.

"We could do dinner here," she said, quieter. "If that's—if you'd be okay with that."

"Yeah." He pulled out the chair across from her usual seat and sat down, unhurried, like he planned to stay. "That sounds good."

She turned toward the stove. Her shoulders dropped half an inch. She reached for the cabinet handle and her hand was almost steady.

1375.scenario:
The corner office smelled like leather and old paper, and Maisie had dragged her imaginary friend Theo all the way up here because she needed someone to talk to while Mom finished her meeting.

Theo perched on the edge of the mahogany desk, watching Maisie pace.

"You know what nobody tells you?" Maisie said, stopping at the window and pressing her nose to the glass. Twenty-three floors below, yellow cabs stuttered through the intersection. "Old people just *stop*. Like a clock. One day you're here and then you're absolutely nowhere, and everyone acts like that's fine." She pulled her nose from the glass and left a small fog-print behind. "It's not fine, Theo. It's the worst thing there is."

But even as she said it, she was drifting toward the framed photographs on the credenza — her mother's boss arranged with his family, generation after generation in matching silver frames. Maisie's eyes moved over the faces the way a tongue finds a sore tooth. She studied the grandmother's jaw, the father's sloped shoulders, the particular way the son's ears sat too low. Her gaze traveled each face methodically, cataloguing, as if she were looking for something she was afraid she might find.

"We should all just *say* it more," she continued, her voice gathering steam. "Instead of whispering at funerals. Instead of changing the subject. Everyone's so scared to just *say* it —" Her finger hovered over the youngest child's photographed face, tracing without touching the curve of the boy's forehead. Her stomach tightened. She pulled her hand back.

"Maisie?" Theo said.

"I'm fine." She turned away from the photographs too quickly, nearly knocking a paperweight off the desk. She steadied it without looking, her eyes already somewhere else — on the window, on the traffic below, on anything that wasn't a face that might reflect something back at her.

"We're all just pretending it won't happen," she said. "That's the real problem. Nobody wants to admit how *fragile* everything is."

She moved to the leather chair in the corner, tucked her knees to her chest, and made herself very small. From there, she couldn't see the photographs.

The taxi smelled like pine air freshener and old upholstery. Maya sat pressed against the door, as far from her father as the backseat allowed, watching the streetlights drag orange streaks across the window.

"People are going to think you planned this," she said, not looking at him. "Showing up to Grandma's dinner in separate cars, forty minutes apart—they're not stupid, Dad. Aunt Renee is going to have *opinions*."

Her father said something quiet and conciliatory. Maya's eyes stayed on the glass.

"And don't even get me started on what the cousins are going to say at school on Monday." She picked at the hem of her sleeve. "I already have to deal with enough."

The driver braked for a yellow light. In the sudden stillness, her foot found her duffel bag on the floor and pressed down on it—checking, the way she'd been checking since they left the house, that it was still there. Both bags. Hers and the overnight one she'd packed without being asked. She'd packed it three weeks ago, actually, and quietly moved it from closet to closet since then, keeping it close, like a small animal she was responsible for.

"Everyone's going to be looking at us," she continued, her voice steady, almost bored. "Wondering."

The light turned green. Her father reached over and touched her shoulder briefly, and Maya went very still—not pulling away, not leaning in. Just waiting to learn what the touch meant. Whether it would stay or retract.

It retracted. He reached for his phone instead.

Her eyes went back to the window. Her foot pressed harder into the bag.

"You should have thought about how it looks," she said.

The break room off the morgue corridor was empty at 2 a.m., which was exactly how Delia preferred it. She sat across from Marcus, her coffee going cold between her palms, the overhead fluorescent humming its single tuneless note.

"I'm just saying," she said, turning her mug in slow circles, "the memorial service is going to be a nightmare. Four hundred people minimum. You know how I get in those situations—I can't breathe, I can't think, everyone pressing in from all sides." She shook her head. "I already told his family I'd sit in the back. Near an exit."

Marcus nodded slowly. He'd heard this before.

What he was watching, though, was her other hand. It had drifted to the sonogram printout on the table between them—the one she'd set face-down when she walked in, as though that made it less present. Her fingers hovered a half-inch above it without touching it, the way you hold your palm over a burner to measure heat. Her eyes never went to it directly, but her body kept orienting toward it the way a compass needle finds north against its will.

"Four hundred strangers all wanting to talk to you," she continued. "Wanting eye contact and handshakes and—" She stopped. Swallowed. Her jaw had gone tight, but not at the thought of the service. Marcus could tell because she only went tight like that when she glanced, involuntarily, at the printout's edge. Each time, her shoulders rose a fraction, her breath went shallow, and she pulled her gaze away as if the paper were a wound she was trying not to probe.

"We could go together," Marcus offered carefully. "To the service."

"God, no." She laughed, and it was almost convincing. "Two anxious people in a crowd is worse than one." She wrapped both hands around the mug now—deliberately, he thought, giving them somewhere to be. "I'd be watching every exit the whole time."

She would. He knew she would.

But she was also, right now, watching the sonogram the same way.

1373.scenario:
The reception hall smelled of lilies and old wood. Margot stood near the casket with a glass of wine she hadn't touched, watching the younger colleagues cluster around the widow—around *her* widow, she caught herself thinking, then felt ashamed.

"It's the Hendricks crowd," she said to Daniel, her voice dropping to something conspiratorial. She tilted her chin toward the far corner, where a group of men in expensive suits had colonized the best chairs. "They're already repositioning. You watch—by the end of the month they'll have rewritten the whole narrative. Edmund will become *their* Edmund." She smoothed the front of her blazer. "I've seen it happen. The people who actually shaped him get quietly edited out."

Daniel nodded, but he was watching her hands.

She had drifted, without seeming to notice, toward the small table where Edmund's books were displayed—a modest memorial arrangement, five titles fanned out beside his photograph. Her fingers found the spine of the first one, *The Meridian Studies*, and stayed there. She wasn't gripping it, exactly. More like confirming it was solid.

"The Hendricks people never respected the work," she continued, scanning the room with the quick, practiced efficiency of someone cataloguing threats. "They respected the *access*. There's a difference." Her gaze snagged on a young woman taking notes on her phone near the widow, and Margot's jaw tightened visibly.

But her free hand had moved to the second book now, *Collected Frameworks*, and she pressed two fingers flat against its cover the way you might press a bruise to make sure it still hurt. She hadn't opened either volume. She didn't need to read them. She needed to feel that they were there, that they had weight, that they occupied space in the world.

"Edmund always said the work outlasts the gossip," she told Daniel. Her voice was steady, even a little arch. "I intend to make sure that's actually true. Someone has to."

She finally looked down at the books beneath her hand—all five of them, their names on the spines, Edmund's name above each title and her own buried in the acknowledgments of three, the footnotes of two—and for just a moment her breath went shallow and her fingers curled, not around the book but around the empty air beside it, as though reaching for a volume that wasn't there.

Then someone across the room laughed too loudly, and her head came up.

"Disgraceful," she said. "At a *wake*."

The community board in the front hallway had been Delia's idea — a corkboard where residents could pin job listings, bus schedules, birthday cards. She'd bought it herself, hauled it up from the dollar store on Clement Street. That was three weeks ago. It was still bare.

Mrs. Okafor found her standing in front of it on a Tuesday evening, thumbtack pinched between two fingers, a flyer for a community garden volunteer day dangling from her other hand.

"You going to pin that up?" Mrs. Okafor asked.

"I'm thinking about it." Delia didn't turn around. Her shoulder blades drew together the moment she heard footsteps, a slow cinching, like curtains being pulled shut. "I just — what if nobody signs up? Then it just hangs there looking sad. Like I put my whole heart into something and nobody cared."

"Someone might care."

"Or they'll walk right past it." Delia's eyes moved along the baseboard, tracked to the stairwell door, drifted to the small window above the mail slots. She shifted her weight to the left, angling her body toward the wall. "That's the thing about trying. You make yourself ridiculous."

Mrs. Okafor waited.

"It's embarrassing," Delia continued, still not turning, "when you reach out and nothing reaches back." The thumbtack pressed into her fingertip — not hard enough to hurt, just enough to feel. Her gaze climbed to the smoke detector on the ceiling, lingered there a beat too long, then dropped back to the flyer. "Anyway. I don't know. Maybe I'll put it up later, when I've — when there's more time."

She folded the flyer in half.

Then in half again.

Then she tucked it into her pocket and walked back down the hall toward her room, keeping close to the wall the whole way, her free hand trailing along the plaster like a guide wire.

The bass hit Marlene in the sternum before she even cleared the venue doors. She stopped walking—just for a half-second—when she saw the cluster of young men near the merchandise table, shirtless and loud, tattoos crawling up their necks. Her hand found Dani's elbow without her seeming to notice she'd reached out.

"Mom, *walk*," Dani said.

Marlene walked. She steered them wide of the cluster, angling toward the far wall, keeping her shoulder to it. One of the men laughed at something, a big bark of sound, and her chin dropped slightly, eyes cutting sideways.

"I'm just saying," she said, raising her voice over the opening act, "we don't think about it. Day to day. We just—we don't. But the bees, Dani. The *bees* are gone. The coral is bleaching. By the time you're my age—"

"Mom."

"—there may not *be* concerts. There may not be venues, or cities, or—" She stopped. A man in a torn jacket had drifted close to them, just someone looking for the bathroom, already gone. Marlene's shoulders had climbed to her ears. She exhaled slowly, deliberately, the way her therapist had shown her, and smoothed the front of her shirt.

"Sorry," she said. "I just want you to understand the stakes."

Dani looked at her mother's hands, still pressed flat against her own stomach, still pressing something down. "I know, Mom," she said, and didn't say anything else.

They found a spot near the back. Marlene kept her eyes on the stage. Every few minutes, without seeming to realize she was doing it, she checked the faces of the people around them—a quick sweep, left to right, settling longest on the men who were big or loud or who stood at the edge of groups. Then she would say something about glaciers.

The trail forked ahead, and Mara stopped walking.

"I don't like this part," she said, pulling her jacket tighter even though the afternoon was warm. "The ranger station guy said there's been people out here—squatters, maybe. Some of them get territorial." She scanned the tree line left, then right, her gaze moving the way a lighthouse beam moves: mechanical, relentless. "You hear about it all the time. Someone just camping and then some guy decides they don't belong."

Priya crouched to retie her boot. "There's nobody out here, Mara."

"You don't know that." Mara's voice was steady, almost instructional. "That's exactly what people say before something happens. We should have told someone our route. Some people don't want witnesses."

Priya straightened and noticed the way Mara was standing—angled slightly sideways, her body a shield aimed at nothing in particular. At Priya, maybe. Her hand kept drifting to the side pocket of her pack and then retreating, like it couldn't decide what it wanted.

"You've got your phone, right?" Mara asked. "Show me it's charged."

Priya held it up. Ninety-one percent.

Mara exhaled—a long, collapsing sound—and for just a moment her eyes closed. Then she glanced at Priya's face the way you check a pulse. Quick. Confirming. She did it again thirty seconds later, when she thought Priya wasn't looking.

"There's a reason you don't hike alone," Mara continued, moving again, walking half a step behind now. "People get weird when they think no one's watching. We just have to be smart." She held a branch back so it wouldn't swing into Priya's path. Held it longer than necessary. "Stay where I can see you, okay? Just—stay close."

1387.scenario:
The departure gate was nearly empty at this hour. Mara set her carry-on down and immediately put eighteen inches of space between herself and Darius, the way water finds a drain—without deciding to.

"People are going to talk," she said, watching the tarmac through the floor-to-ceiling windows. "Your mother's already told half of Riyadh that we left the Hassans' dinner early. Do you know what that looks like? Do you have any idea what they'll say about us?"

Darius scrolled his phone. "It was one dinner."

"It's never *one* dinner." She turned toward him, but her feet stayed planted where they were, angled slightly away, like a door left ajar. "The Hassans have connections to everyone we know. Everyone. We'll be frozen out of the Karimi wedding, the foundation gala—"

A gate agent dropped a clipboard two rows behind them. The sound was nothing. A small, flat crack against linoleum.

Mara's hand shot to the side of her neck.

She stood very still for a moment, her fingertips pressed against her own pulse, her eyes doing a slow, automatic sweep of the gate—the agent, a sleeping businessman, a mother with a stroller, Darius, the agent again—before she let her arm fall.

"—and then what?" she continued, her voice finding its thread again as though the pause had been part of the sentence. "We lose the Farhani account because no one will return our calls, and then your family will blame me. You know they will."

Darius finally looked up. "You're catastrophizing."

"I'm *realistic*." She pulled her boarding pass from her jacket pocket and smoothed it between her thumb and forefinger, over and over, a small repetitive motion she didn't appear to notice she was doing. When he reached out to touch her shoulder, she didn't flinch exactly—it was subtler than that, a kind of preemptive reorganization of her posture, a slight drawing-in, as though her body had already rehearsed the next moment and decided what to do about it.

She stepped toward the window instead.

"Our reputation is the only thing holding this together," she said quietly, fogging the glass a little with her breath. She watched their reflections—him standing, her standing, the careful geography of space between them. "If we lose that, we lose everything."

Outside, a plane taxied slowly away from its gate, its running lights blinking in the dark.

Her hand went back to her neck.

The produce section hummed with refrigeration units and piped-in jazz. Marta spotted Derek before he saw her—she had a habit of cataloguing exit routes when she entered any room, and she'd already noted the gap between the bread display and the dairy coolers when his cart swung around the corner.

"Hey, you," Derek said, stopping. "We missed you at trivia night. Everyone kept asking where you were."

Marta's shoulders dropped half an inch—relief, not tension—and she smiled. "I *told* Rachel I probably couldn't make it. Did she not tell anyone?" She repositioned her cart so the handle faced outward. "I feel terrible. I really do. I hope nobody thought I was blowing them off."

"Nobody thought that." Derek reached past her toward the bagged spinach, and Marta stepped back before his arm had traveled six inches—a clean, automatic retreat, her body solving a problem her mind hadn't registered yet. "We just missed you."

"I should have sent a group text." Her fingers found her cart handle again and gripped it. "I hate when people feel like I don't care." She was already angling slightly toward the aisle's far end, not urgently, just *oriented* that way. When Derek shifted his weight forward to emphasize his next point, her chin lifted and her eyes swept the space around them in a single, practiced arc—the freezer cases, the overhead signage, the nearest gap between displays—before settling back on his face.

"Seriously, no one was upset," he said.

"You're just saying that." She laughed, and it was a real laugh, warm enough. But her free hand had moved to her jacket zipper and was drawing it slowly upward, sealing herself in.

The common room smelled like industrial cleaner and burnt coffee. Maya sat across from Daniel, her fingers laced through his on the laminate tabletop. He'd been admitted three days ago. She'd come every visiting hour.

"I should have noticed sooner," Daniel said, his eyes fixed somewhere past her shoulder. "I keep thinking about it. You were worried and I just—I brushed it off. I made you feel like you were overreacting."

Maya squeezed his hand. "Daniel—"

"No, I mean it." His voice was steady, almost rehearsed. "I didn't want to be a burden on you. I hate that you're the one who had to make the call to my sister. That should never have fallen on you."

A nurse crossed the room behind Maya, clipboard in hand, and Daniel's gaze tracked her automatically—a quick, careful sweep that took in the nurse's path, the other patients at nearby tables, the exit. His shoulders drew slightly inward.

"I just need you to know I'm going to do better," he continued. "For you. I don't want you spending your Tuesdays in a place like this because of me."

The nurse paused near an older man two tables over, asking him something in a low voice. Daniel watched. His thumb had gone still against Maya's knuckles.

"You don't have to worry about me," Maya said softly.

"That's my point exactly." He finally looked at her, and his expression was open, earnest. "You shouldn't have to."

A young patient shuffled past their table, dragging his IV stand. Daniel pulled his hand back from Maya's—not dramatically, just a quiet retrieval—and set it in his lap. He shifted his chair a half-inch to the left, angling himself so the boy's path was clear. His jaw tightened the way it did when he was calculating something.

"Anyway," Daniel said, his voice returning to its careful warmth, "I'm the one who's sorry. That's what I wanted to tell you. I put this on you, and you deserved better than that."

Maya nodded slowly. She didn't say what she was thinking—that he'd rearranged his chair before the boy was even close. That he'd been watching the room since the moment she sat down.

The bass hit Marcus in the chest like a fist as he slid into the booth across from Detective Yuen. He adjusted his collar before sitting—a quick, automatic tug that had nothing to do with the heat—and kept his eyes moving across the crowd. The young ones near the bar, laughing with their whole bodies, barely dressed. He looked at them the way a man looks at a highway he used to know.

"You want to know what kills people in this city?" he said, leaning toward Yuen so she could hear him. "It's not the guns. It's thinking things are gonna get better. Somebody tells you the neighborhood's turning around, the new captain's different, the deal's gonna hold—" He shook his head. "That's the bullet that drops you. The second you start believing something good is coming."

Yuen watched him. His hands were flat on the table, still, but the tendons in his neck moved when the DJ cut the music between tracks and a new song opened with something slower, something that had been popular twenty years ago.

He caught his own reflection in the mirrored column beside them. His jaw tightened. He looked away faster than he'd looked away from anything all night.

"You see Delaney lately?" Yuen asked.

"Don't change the subject." He rubbed the back of his hand absently, knuckles that ached when it rained now. "I'm serious. The most dangerous thing you can sell somebody around here is the idea that waiting pays off. That the next thing is the thing." He laughed, but it came out thin. "Nobody should be walking around with that kind of poison in them."

A woman near the dance floor—mid-forties, maybe, in a dress that fit her beautifully—tilted her head back laughing, and Marcus watched her for three full seconds before he seemed to realize he was doing it. He pulled his gaze back to the table. Straightened the cocktail napkin in front of him. Straightened it again.

"Just—" He exhaled. "Don't let anyone sell you a sunrise, Detective. That's all I'm saying."

The convention floor roared around them—carpet the color of a bruise, booths stacked with glossy brochures nobody would read. Marcus had been talking for four minutes straight, and Deja had counted every one of them.

"I'm just saying," Marcus said, straightening a stack of product samples that didn't need straightening, "my mom's appointment is Thursday. They won't tell you anything over the phone. You call and call and they just—" He laughed, but it landed wrong. "She's seventy-three. Seventy-three. And she lives alone, Deja. What if something happens between now and when I get back? What if she falls and nobody—"

"You booked the next flight out," Deja said gently. "Friday morning."

"Friday morning." He said it like he was testing whether the words were true.

Their regional manager, Phil, materialized from the crowd the way Phil always did—too close, too sudden, already smiling with all his teeth. Marcus turned toward the sound of Phil's footsteps and something shifted in his face, a brief vacancy, as though someone had dimmed him from the inside. He took a single step back, his shoulder blade finding the edge of the display table behind him, and held it there.

"Team!" Phil clapped once. "How are my people?"

"Good," Marcus said. His voice was easy. Practiced. His eyes moved to the nearest exit and back in the time it took Phil to exhale.

"Marcus, buddy, I need you on the floor tomorrow. Seven sharp. Can I count on you?"

"Of course." He was already nodding before the sentence finished—nodding the way you do when you've learned that waiting to answer costs more than agreeing. His hand found the table's edge behind him and gripped it, knuckles going pale.

"Fantastic." Phil squeezed his shoulder on the way past.

Marcus stood very still for a moment after Phil disappeared into the crowd. Then, quietly, he said, "I really need to call my mom tonight."

Deja watched him ungrip the table. Watched him breathe.

"Yeah," she said. "You do."

The creek path was narrow enough that Donna had to walk slightly ahead of Marcus, which she didn't mind. She kept her eyes on the water, pointing out where the bank had eroded since last summer.

"I'm just saying," she continued, stepping over a root without looking down, "that my read on the Hendricks account was completely wrong. I was *sure* they were ready to sign. Completely sure." She laughed, but it came out flat. "That's what scares me, honestly. Not being wrong—I can handle being wrong. It's that I felt so certain. How do you trust your own judgment after that?"

Behind her, Marcus said something reassuring, but Donna had already stopped listening. A man was fishing from the opposite bank, maybe forty yards downstream. Heavyset, camo jacket, a cooler beside him. She registered him before she'd consciously decided to, the way you register a sound before you name it. Her shoulders climbed half an inch. She adjusted her path without comment, angling slightly away from the water's edge.

"And with the Petrov situation—" she went on, her voice easy, professional— "I pushed hard for that partnership because my gut said yes. My gut." She shook her head. "I don't think gut feelings are a reliable instrument. I really don't anymore."

The fisherman reeled in his line. Donna's eyes tracked the movement in her peripheral vision while she gestured with one hand to illustrate her point about Petrov. Her other hand had found the strap of her bag.

Marcus caught up beside her. "You're being too hard on yourself."

"Maybe." She smiled at him. "Or maybe I've just finally gotten honest about how unreliable I am." She glanced back at the bank. The fisherman was standing now. She picked up her pace by half a step, seamlessly, still talking.

"They're relocating the whole fish department to the back of the store next month," Miriam said, adjusting her purse strap. "I heard the manager mention it. 1400.scenario:
The meadow stretched gold and easy in the late afternoon light, but Gerald kept his back to the open field, shoulders pressed against the old fence post where he could see both the tree line and the gravel road at once. His eyes moved in a slow, practiced sweep—tree line, road, tree line, road—while Mrs. Okafor spread her rental agreement across the hood of her car.

"I just want to be clear," he said, and his voice was steady, almost rehearsed. "The lease is twelve months, no exceptions. I've had tenants before who thought they could make the place *feel* like home—bring their families around, expect me to come fix things on holidays, start leaving notes on the door." He shook his head. "That's not what this is."

Mrs. Okafor looked up from the papers. "I just need somewhere to live, Mr. Gerald."

"Good." He nodded sharply. "Keep it simple. Transactional." His gaze snagged on a crow landing in the far grass, and for just a moment his whole body went rigid—shoulders up, jaw locked, one hand gripping the fence post until the knuckles whitened. Then the bird lifted away and something in his chest visibly unknotted.

"I'm not looking for anyone to get attached," he continued, smoothing his jacket with short, compulsive strokes. "Attachment makes people expect things. Makes them *need* things."

He glanced toward the road again. A truck passed in the distance and he tracked it—head turning, eyes narrowing—until it disappeared behind the tree line. Only then did he look back at her.

"Just sign where I've marked," he said quietly. "And we don't have to make it into anything it isn't."

Mrs. Okafor signed. Gerald folded his copy with careful, deliberate hands, but she noticed he positioned himself for the walk back to his car so that nothing—no tree, no tall grass, no blind corner—stood behind him.

1394.scenario:
The bell above the door chimed, and Margot stepped inside, pulling her scarf higher around her throat. She'd been in this shop once before, years ago, with her mother. She remembered the smell—dried chamomile, cedar, something faintly medicinal—and how it had felt then like a place for other kinds of people.

Dex was already at the counter, turning at the sound of the bell. His expression opened into something warm and unguarded.

"Hey." He reached for her arm, a casual greeting, and she stepped just slightly to the side so his hand found air. She glanced toward the window. A woman outside was walking a dog. Just a woman. Nobody she knew.

"I think I'm coming down with something," Margot said, unwinding her scarf with businesslike efficiency. "I wanted to catch it early. That's the only reason I'm here, honestly. I've been reading about elderberry—apparently it cuts the duration significantly."

"I know." Dex watched her. "You mentioned that in your text."

"Well, it's true." She moved toward the wall of tinctures, putting a display of dried herbs between them. Her eyes swept the shop—an older couple near the back, a teenager with headphones. No one who mattered. Her shoulders dropped a half-inch.

"You feeling okay otherwise?" he asked.

"I'm *fine*, I just don't want it turning into something worse." She turned a small amber bottle in her hands without reading the label. "You should probably take some too, honestly. We were in close proximity. That's just—responsible."

Dex leaned against the counter, arms crossed loosely. "Close proximity," he repeated.

"I'm serious. There's something going around." She set the bottle down and picked up another. Her jaw was tight. When the bell above the door chimed again, she turned fast—a sharp pivot, eyes already scanning—then smoothed her expression the moment she saw it was nobody.

"Margot."

"What?"

"The elderberry is on the second shelf. Left side." He paused. "I'm not going to say anything to anyone, if that's what you're worried about."

"My therapist thinks this is good for me," she said, lifting the cue in two pieces and fitting them together with a quarter-turn click. "Getting out. Structured activity. Delia watched from the next table, holding her house cue loosely. "So this is, what, exposure therapy?"

"Does it help?" Delia asked. "Being here?"

Renata chalked the tip in slow, deliberate circles, turning the cue, chalking again. "I think so. I mean, I'm here, right? Six months ago I couldn't even—" She stopped, lining up the break, her elbow dropping into a pendulum she'd spent three weeks correcting. "I couldn't leave the apartment most days."

The break was clean and loud. Two balls dropped.

"That's good," Delia said, and it wasn't entirely clear what she meant.

Renata circled the table without hurrying, reading the spread. She'd been watching tournament footage on her laptop—not to relax, the way she'd told her sister, but to study the way professionals weighted their stance on cut shots. She paused at a difficult angle, one most players would play safe on, and felt the familiar arithmetic assemble itself quietly in her head: speed, english, where the cue ball needed to die.

"The social part is still hard," she said, shooting. The three ball kissed the corner pocket and fell. "I'm working on not catastrophizing when I can't read people." She moved without pausing, already onto the next shot. "Like with you. I never know where we stand."

"We stand here," Delia said. "You beating me."

Renata almost smiled. She was lining up a cross-table shot that had no business working, the kind of shot that required believing in yourself at a cellular level. Dr. Okafor had told her to practice tolerating uncertainty.

She was not thinking about Dr. Okafor.

She shot. The ball traveled the length of the table and disappeared.

"I just think," Renata said, finally looking up, "that if I can get comfortable being around people again, everything else gets easier."

Delia looked at the table. Three balls left, all Renata's.

"Sure," she said. "That's probably it."

The generator died at nine, the way it always did, and Mr. Okafor stood at the edge of the classroom tent in the sudden dark. Around him, the camp settled into its nighttime sounds—distant generators from the medical block, a child crying two rows over, the specific silence of people trying not to be heard.

"Amara." He found her by the orange tip of the battery lantern she always carried. "You should be in your section."

"I was coming to return the geography book." She held it out. Sixteen years old and still believed that rules existed primarily for other people. "Your hands are shaking."

"That I was needed here." He moved to the tent's entrance, where the path between rows of shelters was lit by nothing but a half-moon. He stood there—in the opening, which was the important thing—and kept his eyes on the middle distance. Last month he had not been able to stand in doorways at all. The month before, he had taken the long way around every building rather than pass through a corridor. "She raised me alone. Eleven years, just the two of us. I owe her more than phone calls."

Amara came to stand beside him, following his gaze toward nothing in particular. "My uncle says obligation is just love with the romance taken out."

"Your uncle is a philosopher." Okafor stepped out onto the path. One step, then two, into the open air between the rows of tents pressing close on either side. He breathed. He kept walking, slowly, the way a man walks when he is not fleeing anything. "I send money every month. I arranged a woman to come in the mornings. But she asks when I'm coming home and I—"

He stopped. Amara had stopped too, watching him.

He was standing, he realized, at the narrowest point of the path, canvas walls within arm's reach on both sides, the strip of sky above him thin as a ribbon. He had not crossed to the wider avenue. He had come here on purpose, or something in him had.

"You could go," Amara said. "Visit. They have headmasters in Kampala."

"They have headmasters everywhere." He looked up at the strip of sky. Stars, a few. His breathing was even. He put one hand out and touched the canvas wall beside him, just briefly, just to feel it there and solid and not closing in. "But I made a commitment here. I told the families I would stay through the full year." He lowered his hand. "A person should do what they say they will do."

Amara said nothing, which was occasionally her best quality.

They stood together in the narrow passage for a long moment. Then Okafor straightened, the way a man straightens when something has been settled, and walked the rest of the way through.

She'd spent fourteen of her thirty-one wakeful hours on this part. She'd called three illustrators. She'd sketched out a format in the margins: short chapters, first-person, illustrated pull quotes.

"This is the human hook," she said, tapping the yellow pages. "You lead with the kids. Their voices. The *art* they're making." Her finger moved across a reproduced panel — a girl drawn in thick, earnest lines, standing at the edge of something enormous. Margot had stared at that drawing for a long time in the parking garage before coming upstairs. "This is what makes people care."

"Margot." Denny set down his coffee. "Is this a news story or a middle-grade anthology?"

"It's both," she said, too fast, too certain. "It's how we get to my brother. You run the kids' story first, you establish the publication's presence, *then* we drop the investigative piece and they can't ignore us."

Denny looked at her. She was still touching the yellow pages.

"How's your brother doing?" he asked carefully.

"He's fine, he's—" She pulled her hand back. "He's the reason we need to move quickly. That's what I've been saying."

"The families in my parish," he started.

"Are scared," she finished. "I know. I've talked to them." A pause, just long enough. "Several of them, actually. Maria Esteves. The Okonkwos. They're more flexible than you might think." She said it gently, the way you describe a tree that has already been bent. "People are, when they feel genuinely heard."

He thought about Maria Esteves, who had called him last week sounding somehow less certain than she used to. He thought about the Okonkwos, who had quietly stopped volunteering.
