She nodded, as if this were simply one move in a longer sequence. "Of course. I respect that completely." She pulled out her phone, made a note he couldn't see. "I'm meeting with Bishop Hartley on Thursday. Just so you know. I like to keep everyone informed."

The placemat was a ruin of small torn angles by the time she stood to leave. She hadn't seemed to notice doing it.

"I really do want good things," she said, buttoning her coat. "For everyone. I hope you know that."

Father Mikael looked at the shredded paper on the table after she left. He sat with it for a while. Then he took out his phone and called Maria Esteves, and was surprised to find that she didn't pick up.

She straightened it. Centered it on the table. An absurd, small, honest gesture.

She left the letter in her sleeve. She left the hall. In the corridor, she stopped and pressed her back against the cold stone and thought about the letter, about what it said, about how easy it would have been. How she had the access. How no one would have known.

Cass walked to the base of the ladder and put one hand on the rope, steadying it. She didn't say anything about grandmothers, or compasses, or the particular way a child's voice changes when it's carrying something heavy.

"I need you to commit to this," he said. "I need you to understand that staying where you are is not an option. Not anymore."

"You don't have to stay," she said, without looking up from the contact sheet she was holding to the light. "I know you have the Feldman dinner."

"What is the thread?"

She paused. It was a real pause, not a deflection. "I've been thinking a lot about endings," she said finally. "How a photograph is always a little death. The moment dies so the image can live. I want to make a whole series around that. Cessation. The aesthetics of it." She said it cleanly, like a thesis statement. "I think it's the most honest subject there is."

Dmitri said nothing.

She moved to the next table, where she'd spread out perhaps forty prints, all of them organized in a way that meant something to her. He could see that much. He stood and walked over.

The photographs were of faces. Old faces, mostly—a woman with a jaw like a ship's prow, a man whose ears were enormous and soft-looking, a teenage girl caught mid-laugh with a gap between her front teeth. But scattered among them were other prints: a handprint pressed in clay, a medical diagram of an inner ear, a faded polaroid of a woman he didn't recognize standing in front of a house he didn't recognize, holding an infant wrapped in yellow.

"Who are these people?" he asked.

"I don't know most of them." She moved two prints two inches to the left, then back. "That's sort of the point."

She reached out and touched the edge of the polaroid—not the image itself, but the white border, as if the image were too warm to handle directly.

"The series is about dissolution," she said. "About how a self just—stops. How that's actually fine. Natural." She looked up at him briefly. "I think people make too much of continuity."

Then she turned back to the table and rearranged three more prints, building a loose triptych: the woman with the ship's-prow jaw, the polaroid, and a close-up of an eye—brown, with a dark ring at the iris—that Dmitri realized, slowly, looked something like Mara's own.

She didn't seem to notice she'd done it.

She stood there for a long moment, her fingertip resting on the eye print, her face very still and very open in a way it almost never was.

"I just want to make something true," she said quietly, to the photographs more than to him. "Before it doesn't matter anymore."

When she finally took it—two-handed, formal, like accepting a treaty—he felt something shift behind his sternum that he would have had real difficulty naming.

Selin was watching him from across the yard. He raised the clipboard like a shield.

"I'm not asking you to fix it." She turned back to the water. "I just think you deserve to know. You've worked so hard with me." She let the sentence breathe. Watched him lean forward in her peripheral vision.

She had told her sister the same thing last Tuesday. Her mother on Thursday. She kept a mental ledger of their responses—who called back fastest, who cried, who made her promise things. The promises were the most useful part. *Promise me you won't. Promise me you'll call.* Each one a small thread she could hold.

"I want you to feel like you can tell me anything," Dr. Ferris said carefully. "But I also need to ask about your safety plan."

"I threw it away," she said. She hadn't. It was folded in her wallet, behind her library card. But she watched his hand move toward his phone, watched him recalculate, watched him become entirely, usefully focused on her.

The ocean did its slow work at the shoreline. Marlene breathed in the salt air and felt, for the first time that week, that she was not disappearing. She was, in fact, the most solid thing on the beach.

"I don't know how much longer I can do this," she said quietly, and reached over to touch his arm before he could reach for his phone—a gesture that looked like comfort, that *was* comfort, of a kind, though not the kind he would have named.

He stilled. She had known he would.

Mara's hand moved to her jacket pocket—the one with the drive. She didn't take it out. She just rested her fingers against it the way you'd rest a hand on a sleeping child's back, just to feel the breathing.

"The guest room," Dani said. "In Portland."

"Yeah."

"What's it like?"

Mara opened her mouth. Closed it. She was looking at the building again. Ninth floor, third window from the left, the one with the faint blue equipment glow behind the blinds. Someone was still in there. She was calculating, automatically, whether that changed anything.

"Yellow curtains," she said, distantly. "My sister says they're cheerful."

Dani watched her. Mara's fingers pressed harder against the drive.

"When are you telling Vasquez?" Dani asked.

"Tomorrow," Mara said. "After."

She hadn't meant to say the last word. It arrived on its own, the way true things do.

Dani looked at the building. Looked at Mara. Didn't say *after what*, because she already knew, and maybe that was the thing about Dani that made Mara's chest ache—she always already knew.

"I'll go with you," Dani said. "To Vasquez."

"Yeah?"

"After."

Mara finally looked at her. The lights moved in the water. Her hand stayed where it was.

"The curtains are ugly, actually," Mara said. "But my sister tried."

"You don't have to jump," he said, which was the third time he'd said it. Each time, he watched her shoulders drop a little further.

"Of course not." He smiled at her back. "You've always been braver than me."

"No, hey." He raised both hands. "I told you. You don't have to. This was your idea."

It hadn't been her idea.

Dani stared at the water.

Her grandfather was the person she admired most in the world. She'd told Marcus that once, in a fight, meaning it as a wound. He had filed it away.

"I'm going to jump," she said.

"Dani—"

"I want to."

He watched her step back to the edge. He watched her breathing change, watched her gather herself in the particular way she had, chin dropping, weight shifting forward. He felt something loosen pleasantly in his chest — not pride, though it resembled pride — the specific satisfaction of watching someone override themselves.

"I don't need to be here long," she said, without turning around. "I just think — you know what the therapist said. That I'm too hard on myself about the accident. About the whole year, really." She paused at a water-damaged copy of *Gray's Anatomy*, flipped it open. "I'm trying to practice just... letting things go. Being gentler."

"Okay," Declan said. He shifted the coats to one arm.

Mara set the anatomy book down, then immediately picked it up again and tucked it under her elbow. Her eyes had already moved on — to a stack of National Geographics, to a cracked-spine field guide to North American birds, to what looked like an old pharmacology manual with a red sticker on the cover.

"The accident wasn't my fault. I know that now. Or I'm learning it." She reached past a ceramic owl to pull the pharmacology manual free. "That's really all this is. Just me working on being okay with myself again."

Declan watched her open the manual to a dog-eared page and read for a moment, her lips slightly parted, her whole body going still the way it only did when she found something that interested her.

"You want a basket?" he asked.

"No, I'm not buying anything." She turned a page. Then another. Her thumb found the corner of a third. "It's not about accumulating things. It's about the practice of showing up. Being present without judgment."

She made her way to the National Geographics without looking up from the manual.

"Declan, there's a whole run of these from 1987. That's the year they did the—" She crouched down, balancing the pharmacology book on her knee, pulling issues out with her free hand to check the dates. "There was an article on cave systems in the Yucatán. I read about it somewhere. If they have March—"

"I'll get a basket," he said.

"I don't need a basket." She found March. Her face opened like a window. "I just need to be easier on myself."

"Maybe. Or maybe I'd discover something." She stopped at the oldest pear, the one he'd entered in the regional show four years running. Her hand rested on a branch he'd spent a decade coaxing horizontal. "I think I need to start making real decisions. Not just executing yours."

Ellard straightened slowly. "We have the new beds. You could—"

"The new beds are clay and shade." She said it without heat, just a statement of fact. "I'd like to try with the established stock. Just one tree, to start. To see what I do when it's actually mine."

He was quiet for a moment. A crow landed on the fence post and left.

"That's a reasonable thing to want," he said finally.

Priya nodded, already lifting the shears toward a branch he'd never have touched—a load-bearing limb, structural, the one that made the whole form possible. She cut with confidence, the way she'd watched him cut a hundred times, the way she'd practiced until his technique lived in her hands like memory.

"I think that's what this whole apprenticeship has been building toward," she said, stepping back to look at the wound she'd made. "Just figuring out who I actually am."

"Getting ready," she said, without looking up.

She glanced at the notepad, then at him. "So I can help you talk about it. In the group. So you have somebody to practice with first."

"I just need to fix it," she told Dr. Osei. "That's all this is. I got it wrong the first time — the ending, the structure, the whole second act. Patrick said as much. My editor said as much." She laughed, short and airless. "Honestly, everyone said as much."

Dr. Osei nodded. "And what would fixing it look like?"

"Mm." He watched her thumb the page open.

She looked down at it. Her own handwriting filled the margins — not edits, but questions. *What did she keep in the attic? Why does she hum that specific song?* Small archaeological notations, the kind you leave when you suspect there's more ground to dig.

"Patrick says readers won't follow her logic," Miriam continued. "And he's probably right. She behaves — I don't know. Strangely. She doesn't explain herself." A pause. "Which is maybe the most honest thing about her."

"Do you want to cut her?"

Miriam's grip tightened on the page. "I want to stop defending choices I can't justify." She turned the sheet over, and there was a new paragraph she'd drafted by hand, dense and careful, the letters pressed hard into the paper the way people write when they're trying not to lose something. "I've been doing that for months. Justifying. It's exhausting."

"What's that?" Dr. Osei asked, nodding at the handwritten paragraph.

She looked at it as if she'd forgotten she was holding it. "Nothing. A passage. I was on the train this morning." She set it face-down on top of the stack, then immediately picked it back up. "It's the mother. In the attic. I think I finally understand what she's been doing up there."

She said nothing else for a moment, reading her own words, her thumb moving slowly along the bottom edge of the page.

"I should probably just cut her," she said.

Delia exhaled. "Thank you. We just get her, that's all. We get her and we leave."

"Sure." He was already mentally mapping the building—not the stairwell door she'd mentioned, but the electrical panel on the second floor, the one with the loose cover and the exposed wiring he'd noticed on a job last spring. He'd thought about it since then, the way the whole corridor would go dark.

"You understand, right? In and out. No trouble."

"No trouble," he agreed, and smiled at her, and meant it the way he meant most things—partially, provisionally, in the fraction of himself that was paying attention to her at all.

He'd slipped that last one into the front pocket.

"The therapeutic goal," he told Hargrove as they reached the survey site, "is really just to stop letting the diagnosis feel like the whole story." He set down his bag and unzipped it. The primer page crinkled softly at the top of the pocket. "To see myself more clearly, I guess. More accurately."

1786.dialogue_answer: reconciling with an estranged family member

The dryers were going when Marta came in, and the noise covered the sound of her crying, which she appreciated.

She'd stopped crying by the time her neighbor Cal pushed through the glass door with his laundry bag. He nodded at her. She nodded back. He loaded his machine and sat two plastic chairs down from her.

"Haven't seen you around," he said, not unkindly.

"I've been—" She smoothed her jeans over her knees. "I've been trying to get in touch with my brother. We haven't really spoken in eight years."

"That's a long time."

"It is." She looked at her hands. "I keep thinking, if I could just sit across from him. Have a meal. I don't need him to apologize or anything. I just want to see his face." She paused. "Make sure he knows I don't blame him."

Cal nodded slowly. "You reach out?"

"I wrote a letter." She'd addressed it last Tuesday, then left it on the counter for four days before dropping it in the box this morning. "I don't know if he'll answer."

"He might."

"He might," she agreed.

The machines hummed. Outside, a truck downshifted on the wet street, and Marta watched it pass the window with a focused, almost hungry attention — the way it moved through the intersection without slowing, the indifferent weight of it.

She'd chosen this laundromat because it was across town. She'd walked here along the bridge, and she had stood at the railing for a while, watching the dark water below catch the streetlights. She hadn't decided anything. She'd just stood there, breathing, until a cyclist startled her moving again.

"Family's complicated," Cal offered.

"It is." She pulled her damp clothes from the washer and loaded the dryer, feeding quarters in one by one. She'd brought exact change. She'd brought only exact change — nothing extra in her pockets, her wallet left at home, her phone uncharged and face-down in her apartment.

The letter was real. She meant every word of it.

"I just want him to know I'm thinking about him," she said. "Before—" She stopped.

Cal looked at her.

"Before too much more time passes," she finished.

She sat back down. She watched the dryer window, the slow turn of her clothes in the heat, and she looked almost peaceful — the way people look when they have finally, quietly, made room for something.

Her mother looked down at her hands. Then, almost involuntarily, she glanced at the bag—caught herself doing it—and looked back up.

"I want something quiet," she said. "That's the whole point. Four walls, a door that locks, nothing complicated." She tapped the simplest floor plan with one finger. "I've been in this industry long enough to know what happens to people who keep pushing their luck. I'm not doing that anymore."

The contractor, a heavyset man named Bryce, studied the plan. "This lot's a good choice. Backs up to the tree line. Private."

"Exactly." She nodded like he'd confirmed something important. "I want out of the city. Out of the whole — scene. Fresh start."

Bryce pulled out his notepad. "Any special requests? Materials, layout?"

She said no without hesitating. Then, after a pause, asked if the master bedroom could face east.

He wrote it down. "Any reason?"

"Light," she said, and left it there.

But while he flipped through the spec sheets, she drifted to the window. Through the mud and scaffolding she could see the rough framing of the structure next door — and she stood there watching a worker carry a beam across his shoulders the same way her brother used to, same tilt, same roll of the left shoulder compensating for an old injury. She watched until the man turned and the resemblance dissolved.

"The closet space," she said, returning to the table. "I'll need more than this shows. I'm keeping some things."

Bryce glanced up. "Storage unit might be cheaper than square footage."

"No." She said it quickly, then softened it. "I want it in the house. I want to know where everything is."

He shrugged and made a note. She looked back at the floor plan — the clean lines, the single occupancy, the efficient absence of extra rooms — and described it to him as exactly what she'd always wanted. A place designed for one person, by choice, going forward.

She asked, almost as an afterthought, whether the contractor could source reclaimed oak for the floors. Bryce said it was possible but expensive.

"That's fine." She touched the edge of the blueprint. "My father had floors like that."

Diane had told herself she'd drink through it—that was her plan, the whole architecture of the night—but instead she'd spent forty minutes rearranging the complimentary toiletries on the bathroom counter, and now she was standing in the open doorway of room 214 while Marcus, who had beaten her for the Caldwell Prize three years running, stood in the hallway in his undershirt holding an ice bucket.

"I'm getting through it," she said, which was how she'd answered his question about whether she was okay. "That's all I'm doing. Getting through."

He nodded. He didn't say *through what.* They both knew about her brother.

"I don't need company," she added. "I'm not one of those people."

Marcus looked at the ice bucket. She looked at the ice bucket. Neither of them moved.

"I have two glasses," she said. "Stupid. They always give you two."

"That's just how they make the rooms."

"It's a waste is what it is." She stepped back from the doorway—not quite an invitation, not quite not one. "I've been reading his letters. That's how I'm handling it. Very controlled. Very—" She gestured vaguely at the room, at the letters fanned across the bedspread, at the methodical grief she had arranged like evidence. "I have a system."

Marcus set the ice bucket down inside the door. He looked at the letters, then at the two glasses on the nightstand, then at her.

"I'll just sit," he said. "I'm not good at talking."

"Good," Diane said. "I don't want to talk."

She picked up one of the letters. He pulled the chair from the desk to a reasonable distance from the bed and sat down. For a while the only sound was the ice settling.

She read. He stayed.

After some time she said, without looking up, "There's a vending machine down the hall. He liked those orange crackers. The ones with peanut butter."

"I know the ones."

"They're terrible."

"They're really not great," Marcus agreed.

She turned a page. "Room 214," she said. "If you forget."

He didn't say anything. He didn't leave either.

"I just want my life back," he said, quieter now. "Is that so hard to understand? I want to wake up in the morning and not be anybody's asset."

"I know." She put a hand briefly on his arm. "I know that's what you want."

She'd been tracking his movements for eleven days now — not obsessively, she told herself, just carefully — and she had his rhythms memorized the way you memorize a song you never meant to learn.

She slid into the water and moved toward him.

"Declan." She said his name like she'd only just remembered it. "I've been meaning to find you. About the Whitmore account."

He turned. Something crossed his face — not quite fear, but its polite cousin.

"Marta." He set down his glass. Sparkling water with lime. She'd noticed that too.

"The board is going to ask questions," she said, settling onto the submerged stool beside him. "If you're not there to answer them, the losses get attributed to you personally. You understand that, right? Everything you have." She spread her hands, gesturing at the resort, the palms, the enormous blue sky. "Gone."

He looked at her steadily. "You came all the way to Phuket to tell me that."

"Someone had to."

He nodded slowly, picked up his glass again, turned it in his hands without drinking from it. Just held it. She watched his thumb trace the condensation on the side, slow and deliberate, like a man reassuring himself about something.

"I'm not coming back early," he said. "Not yet."

"The shareholders—"

"Marta." His voice was quiet. "I know what's at stake financially. I do. But I need two more weeks."

She leaned forward. "Two weeks is the difference between a settlement and a lawsuit. You know that."

"Yes." He looked out at the water. "I know."

A waiter appeared and Declan ordered another sparkling water — his fourth, she'd counted — and when it arrived he wrapped both hands around it like it was the only solid thing for miles. Not drinking it. Just holding it. His knuckles were pale.

She should have felt the advantage of this moment. She'd engineered it carefully enough. But something about the way he was gripping that glass made her hesitate.

"Two weeks," he said again, almost to himself.

She thought about the eleven days she'd spent watching him. How he'd switched tables at dinner to sit farther from the resort bar. How he took the long path back to his villa, the one that didn't pass the lounge. How he'd stood at the edge of the ocean yesterday for forty minutes, just standing there, doing nothing, like a man practicing something.

"Two weeks," she finally said, and she wasn't sure anymore whether she was agreeing or just repeating the only thing in the conversation that felt true.

Delia looked up from her phone, then back down. "Dad."

"I heard you joined that church group." He unwrapped his plastic fork with the patience of someone who had nowhere else to be. He'd driven forty minutes for this. "The one that does the sunrise prayer things."

"Youth group. Yeah."

"I'm not attacking it." He held up both hands, a gesture she didn't see because she was still looking at her phone. He noticed she'd cut her hair since August. He noticed she was wearing the bracelet her mother had given her. He filed these things away. "I just think it's worth asking — when they tell you what to believe, do they ever explain *why*? Delia set her phone face-down. That was something, at least. "It's not like that."

"I went through a phase like this," he said. "Needed something solid to hold onto. Totally get it. I'm just saying, the people who are most certain are usually the ones who've never had anyone really push back on them." He speared a piece of melon. "Certainty's a fragile thing. One good question and it tends to just..." He opened his hand. "Dissolve."

She was watching him now. That was something too.

"So what's your good question?" she asked.

"Oh, I've got several." He smiled. "But I want to hear yours first. What do *you* actually believe? Not what Pastor Kevin says. You."

She opened her mouth.

He leaned forward — just slightly, just enough — and his coffee cup bumped her phone and he grabbed it before it fell, and when he handed it back his fingers covered hers for a moment longer than necessary, and he didn't notice he'd done it, and she did.

"I believe," she said slowly, "that you didn't drive here to talk about church."

He leaned back. Picked up his fork again. "I drove here because you stopped returning my calls. I'm trying to understand what's going on with you."

"By dismantling my beliefs."

"By *talking* to you." His voice was even, reasonable, the voice of a man making a fair point. Under the table his leg was bouncing. He'd texted her seven times since Tuesday. He'd driven past her school on Wednesday, told himself he was in the neighborhood. "Someone has to ask you hard questions, Delia. That's what I'm here for. That's what a parent does."

She looked at him for a long moment.

"You haven't asked me a single question about my life," she said. "You've been here ten minutes."

He opened his mouth to explain what he was really doing, what she wasn't understanding, how this was all in service of her thinking for herself — and then his phone lit up on the table between them and she could see before he flipped it over that he'd had a notification: *Delia Marchetti tagged in a photo.*

She'd posted something that morning. He'd had alerts on.

"Dad," she said, quieter now.

"The church thing genuinely concerns me," he said.

1874.scenario:
The bonfire had been going for two hours before Renata finally found Marcus sitting apart from the others, near the waterline where the sand was dark and wet.

"You've barely moved," she said, dropping down beside him.

"I'm watching the bioluminescence." He pointed at the faint blue-green pulses where the small waves broke. "It's dinoflagellates. Single-celled organisms that emit light when they're disturbed. I read about it, but I wanted to see it firsthand." He paused. "That's why I wanted to come tonight. I knew this beach would have them."

Renata nodded slowly. She'd believed him when he said it, back when he'd lobbied to join the party. She still mostly believed him.

"What's the trigger?" she asked. "For the light."

"Mechanical stress. Anything that disrupts the membrane." He picked up a small stone and tossed it underhand into the surf. A brief scatter of cold light bloomed and faded. "See? You can learn a lot just by introducing a variable and observing the response."

"That's very scientific of you."

He smiled, but his hands were already doing something else — turning a smooth piece of sea glass over and over between his fingers, the same repetitive motion she'd noticed him use in the car, and at dinner last week, and on the three occasions she'd found him standing in the kitchen at midnight, just standing, touching the edge of the counter. He didn't seem to know he was doing it.

"I've been reading about perception, too," he said. "How the brain constructs reality. There's this thing where — if you're exposed to a stimulus long enough, you stop registering it. Habituation. Your nervous system just decides it's background noise."

"Mm." She watched his thumb move across the glass. Back and forth. The rhythm of it was almost tidal.

"I want to understand how that works. Why certain things get filtered out and others don't." He looked at the water. "Why some signals keep breaking through no matter what."

The stone in his hand caught the firelight from behind them. He turned it again. She thought about saying something — not about the stone, but about the appointment she'd made for him, the one she hadn't told him about yet, with the doctor his father had finally agreed to. She thought about how to begin that conversation.

"Cold?" she asked instead.

"A little." He didn't move.

She stayed beside him, and neither of them spoke for a while, and the small waves kept disturbing the dark water, and the light kept appearing and disappearing, and Marcus kept turning the glass in his hands like a question he hadn't figured out how to ask.

The judge's chambers smelled of old paper and lemon polish. Mara sat across from her grandmother, who had driven three hours to be here, and tried to remember that she'd agreed to this meeting voluntarily.

"I just want you to understand why I filed the restraining order," Mara said, folding her hands on the mahogany table. "Against Dad. Not against you. I need you to know the difference."

Her grandmother, Bette, nodded slowly. Her knuckles were swollen around her rings. Mara noticed, the way she always noticed now — cataloguing the woman's joints, her gait, the slight tremor that had appeared sometime around Christmas.

"I've been in therapy for two years," Mara continued. "And what I'm working on — what I'm *finally* working on — is learning that not everyone is going to hurt me. That I can let people in." She looked at the judge's empty chair rather than at Bette. "That's why I'm here. That's what this is about."

Bette said, "I know, sweetheart."

"Because I *want* a relationship with you. I want to stop flinching every time someone raises their voice." Mara's jaw tightened. "I deserve that. My therapist says—"

"Mara."

"She says the first step is naming what I need, so I'm naming it. I need safety. I need—"

"Mara." Bette touched her wrist. "How are you getting home tonight?"

The question landed wrong, too small for the room. Mara blinked. "What?"

"It's supposed to ice over. Route 9 gets bad."

"I'm — I'll be fine. Gran, I'm trying to tell you something important."

"I know you are." Bette didn't move her hand.

Mara looked down at it. The swollen knuckles. She thought about the drive Bette had made, three hours, alone. She thought about whether Bette had eaten. Whether the hip was still bothering her. Whether anyone had checked.

"Are you staying at the Marriott on Clement?" Mara asked.

"The Comfort Inn. It's cheaper."

"The Comfort Inn doesn't have an elevator." Mara was already reaching for her phone. "You can't do the stairs with your hip. I'll find you somewhere else, I'll—" She stopped. Looked up. Became, briefly, aware of herself.

She set the phone down.

"Sorry," she said. "You were listening. I was — sorry."

Bette smiled, not unkindly. "Book me the room," she said. "Then tell me about your therapist."

Mara looked at her grandmother's hands for another moment. Then she picked up the phone.

"Your family took everything good from mine," she told Maren, her voice even, almost reasonable. "This is just—correction."

She began to grind.

The paste that formed was not meant to balance anything. It was meant to spread. She'd already spoken to the alderman's cook, to the woman who supplied the church with communion wine, to the boy who delivered water to the schoolhouse. Small agreements. Small doors left unlocked.

"I don't enjoy this," Liss said, which was true in the way that many true things are incomplete.

Her hands kept moving, pressing the pestle down in slow, deliberate circles, working the darkness into something that could be carried, poured, passed hand to hand without anyone quite knowing what they were passing.

Mira's eyes drifted to them now—just for a second—and then she looked back at her worksheet.

She picked up a new pencil and sounded out the first word slowly, her finger underneath each chunk the way Ms. Farrow had shown her. *Re. mem. ber.* She wrote it in the margin for practice.

"The chunking thing is actually starting to work," she told Pip quietly. "I could feel it on the last paragraph."

Pip made a small, skeptical noise only she could hear.

"Okay, *also,*" Mira muttered, "Destiny does this thing where she looks at you after, like, *well?* And I don't like that look. I don't like how it makes me feel like I have to." She pressed her lips together. "But that's not the main thing. The main thing is reading practice."

She turned back to the worksheet.

She stayed with it anyway, not because Ms. Farrow was watching, but because the worksheet was *hers* and the afternoon at Destiny's house would have been something else entirely.

"I'm getting better," she told Pip.

He curled a little closer, which was his way of saying *yes, and also I see you.*

"My ex used to say I was the kind of person who needed a guide for everything," she told Jonas, pulling ahead on the switchback. "Like I couldn't read a map. Like I'd just wander into a ravine." She laughed, short and sharp. "I've done eleven trails this year."

"This part's a little exposed," he said.

"It's fine," she said. "I've done worse."

She had. She knew she had. But she reached out anyway and touched two fingers to his elbow — barely anything, just a graze — and he adjusted his pace to match hers without comment, without making it a thing, and something in her chest went very quiet.

"He used to say I was too cautious," she continued, because silence still made her nervous. "That I'd never push myself. That I'd always need someone holding my hand." She said the last words with a small, defiant lift of her chin.

Jonas glanced at her fingers, still resting at the crook of his arm.

He didn't say anything. He just didn't move away.

They walked like that until the path widened again, and when it did, Mara didn't immediately let go.

1877.scenario:
The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and wet dog. Priya sat rigid in the plastic chair, her rescue greyhound Biscuit pressed against her shins, and watched Derek come through the glass door with his cat carrier.

Of course it was Derek.

He spotted her and did the same small flinch she did, then recovered into a smile. "Hey." He settled into the chair across from her, setting the carrier on his lap. "Didn't know you came here."

"Just started." She scratched behind Biscuit's ears. The dog's narrow head swiveled toward the door every time it opened, tracking each arrival. "New vet. New everything, kind of. That's the whole point."

"Right, yeah. You mentioned you were doing the program thing."

"Ninety days." She said it the way people say a number they've rehearsed. "My sponsor says routine is the whole game. Same grocery store, same coffee place, same vet. You build a life that holds you, you know? Brick by brick." She'd clearly said this before. It sounded true when she said it.

Derek nodded slowly. "That's good, Priya. That's actually really good."

Biscuit made a low sound, not quite a whine. Priya's hand moved automatically to the dog's collar — not petting, holding. Her eyes had drifted to the door again.

"So how's—" Derek started.

"Do you ever feel like you just needed to *go*?" she said, still watching the entrance. "Like the whole reason I got Biscuit was so I'd have a reason to leave the apartment. To actually *move*. My therapist thinks it's about building structure, and she's probably right, but—" She stopped. Biscuit had pressed harder into her legs, and she let him. "He does this thing where he finds my feet in the dark. Like he's checking."

"Checking what?"

She looked at Derek for the first time since he'd sat down. "That I'm still there, I guess."

Her phone buzzed. She glanced at it, then tucked it face-down in her pocket without reading it. Her knee was bouncing.

"Anyway." She sat up straighter. "Ninety days is the foundation, that's what they say. After that you start actually building." She smiled, and it was a real smile, just slightly too wide. "Brick by brick."

Biscuit faced the door. Priya's hand stayed on his collar.

1889.scenario:
The cellar was cool and close, and Marcus had been talking for twenty minutes about his ex-wife.

"She never understood it," he said, pulling a bottle from the rack without looking at the label. "The drinking, I mean. She called it a problem. But some people just—" He waved the bottle. "Some people need an edge taken off, you know? That's all this is."

Celeste watched him. She'd come down here because he'd promised her a 1998 Barolo, and also, she supposed, because she hadn't wanted the night to end yet. She wasn't sure which reason was more honest.

"She sounds like she was difficult," Celeste said, which wasn't what she thought.

"Impossible." Marcus finally looked at the label, set that bottle back, chose another. "I'm better this way. Honestly. Alone. No one monitoring every glass." He laughed, short and dry. "This is better."

But even as he said it, he was doing the thing Celeste had noticed him doing all evening—running his thumb along the wine rack's wooden slats, slow and deliberate, the way you'd read Braille. He'd done it at dinner too, with the tablecloth. With the rim of her glass before he'd handed it to her.

He pulled the cork and poured without ceremony, then stood in the amber light holding both glasses and looking at her with an expression he probably didn't know he had. Careful. Attentive. The face of someone conducting an experiment they're afraid to name.

"You're going to tell me what you taste," he said. "Not what you're supposed to taste. What you actually taste."

"Why?"

"Because—" He stopped. Handed her the glass. "I've been making this blend for three years and no one's ever given me a straight answer."

Celeste took a sip. He watched her mouth.

"You're not alone because it's better," she said.

"I know," he said, quietly, not arguing. He was still watching her face like it was a page he needed to memorize.

He hadn't asked the teacher to come here, exactly — he'd just said *come by the house* — and now he watched her glance around like she was trying to read the room.

"I've given thirty-one years to that district," he said. He picked up a socket wrench and turned it over in his hands, not using it, just holding it. "Thirty-one years, and they want me out the door with a plaque and a handshake. That's not how this works."

"I'm asking you to back me up at the board meeting. You were there. You saw what I built." He set the wrench down in its exact spot on the pegboard, adjusting it a quarter inch until the silhouette matched. "They owe me the directorship. It doesn't go to some outside hire. That's not what I earned."

She watched him drift to the far wall without seeming to notice he was doing it. An old desk sat there, buried under folders and binders, and he began straightening them — gently, almost tenderly — into a neat stack. On top was a photograph in a cracked frame: a younger man in a shop class, students crowded around a half-built engine. Hargrove's father, she realized. Same jaw.

"The vocational program," he said, still not looking at her. He smoothed the corner of a folder. "If they bring in their person, it's gone. First thing. I've seen how they operate." He finally looked up. "I built that program from nothing. Same as he did." He stopped, seemed to catch himself, and his voice hardened again. "Point is, they can't just move me aside. I won't let them take what I've put in."

Ms. Okafor looked at the photograph, then at his hands still resting on the folders.

"What does the directorship actually let you do?" she asked quietly. "That you can't do now?"

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Looked down at the stack of binders — thirty years of curriculum, she realized, student records, lesson plans, his father's original course outlines tucked underneath.

"Protect it," he finally said. Then, as if remembering his argument: "And I've *earned* that right."

"Anyway," she said.

She teed up her own ball. Her practice swing was good. The real one wasn't; she'd glanced sideways at him halfway through. The ball dribbled forty yards.

She laughed first. Loudly. Watching his face to see if he'd laugh too.

He did, and something in her posture changed — shoulders dropping, chin lifting — the whole architecture of her body rearranging itself around that small sound from him.

"I just think it's better for everyone if we're honest," she said, pulling her tee from the ground. "I know what I want."

She said it to the grass, not to him. Then she looked up, quickly, to check if he was still watching her.

He was.

She smiled before she could decide to.

The helicopter banked hard over the mountain range, and Sergeant Delacroix gripped the overhead strap without thinking, steadying herself before her stepson could notice.

Marcus noticed.

"You can just hold on," he said through the headset. "Everyone holds on."

"I'm fine." She released the strap and folded her hands in her lap. "Walk me through the instrument panel again. The altimeter — that's this one?"

Marcus leaned across her and pointed. He'd been a flight instructor for three years now, and she'd asked him to take her up six times in the past four months. She always arrived with a yellow legal pad covered in questions. *What does the collective do? How do you read the horizon in low visibility? What happens if both engines fail simultaneously?*

"Mom," he said, and she stiffened slightly at the word, still not used to it after twelve years. "You've asked me about the altimeter before."

"I want to understand it better." She uncapped her pen. "Depth of understanding, not just surface familiarity."

He nodded and explained it again. She wrote things down.

What she didn't write down: which gauges he checked first during startup, and in what order. The way his hands moved before he touched any control — a half-second of stillness, like a decision. She'd been watching that. She'd been watching which switches he reached for without looking, which ones required his eyes.

After they landed, she asked if she could borrow his ground school manuals.

"You want to take the written exam?" he asked, surprised.

"I want to understand what you do," she said. "You've built something here. I want to understand it properly."

He handed her the manuals. She thanked him and tucked them under her arm.

In the car, before she started the engine, she opened to the chapter on solo certification requirements and read it twice.

The chandeliers at the Hargrove Foundation Gala threw warm light across the room, and Miriam had already refilled her champagne twice by the time she spotted her tenant, Daniel, near the silent auction tables.

She crossed the parquet floor toward him, smoothing her gown. He looked up from a framed watercolor he'd been inspecting and smiled.

"Miriam. Didn't expect to see you here."

"Likewise." She accepted his handshake, held it a beat too long. "How are things? At the unit, I mean."

"Fine, fine." He gestured vaguely. "Actually, I've been meaning to call you. About the lease renewal—"

"Right, yes." She nodded, but her eyes had already drifted past him to the watercolor he'd been examining. She tilted her head slightly, reading the artist's name. "I've actually been doing a lot of work on myself lately. My therapist—I finally started seeing someone—she says the anxiety I have around, you know, *control*, that it's worth unpacking. That I need to practice letting go." She laughed softly, a practiced sound. "So I'm trying."

"That's great," Daniel said, genuinely. "It takes courage."

"It does." She nodded again, more firmly this time, as if agreeing with herself. Then: "Did you ever get that drip under the kitchen sink sorted? Because if there's moisture sitting under the cabinet—"

"I put a call in to the plumber last week—"

"Which plumber?" Her champagne flute hovered halfway to her lips. "Not the one on Clement Street, I hope. He patched something in unit four and the whole subfloor—" She stopped herself. Smiled. "Sorry. I'm working on that. The, uh, catastrophizing." She touched her collarbone lightly. "My therapist calls it 'intrusive maintenance spirals.' Apparently it's a thing."

Daniel's expression was kind, careful. "I'll send you the receipt. Everything's fine."

"No, I know. I know it is." She exhaled slowly, the way someone does when they've been taught to exhale slowly. "I'm just—I'm in a process right now. Learning to trust that things hold together even when I'm not watching." She glanced past his shoulder toward the exit, where the coat check was, where she'd left her bag—the bag that contained, she was now thinking, the spare key to the building she hadn't been able to make herself remove from her keychain.

She brought her gaze back to Daniel and smiled warmly.

"You look well," she said. "Are you enjoying the gala?"

"Very much." He nodded at the watercolor. "I was thinking about bidding on this one, actually. For the living room."

Something moved across her face—quick, involuntary, gone. "You're allowed to hang things, you know. Within reason. Nothing that would—" She pressed her lips together. Set her champagne down on a passing tray. "You know what, never mind. Get the painting. It's lovely."

Her brother would be in town in four days.

She had not thought about what she would show him.

The fire investigator had cleared the porch, so Delia and Marcus stood in the yard, watching smoke still curl from the second-story windows of what used to be her house.

"Insurance will cover the structure," Marcus said. He was her mentor, had been for eleven years, and he spoke in the careful way he always did when he was doing math out loud. "The real question is contents. Do you have your policy number somewhere?"

"In my email." Delia was staring at the upstairs window. Her old bedroom. Her mother's old bedroom, technically—Delia had just never bothered to change which room she slept in after her mother left.

"Okay. And the camera equipment?"

"Itemized. I did it last spring, like you told me." She pulled out her phone, but instead of opening email, she stood there with it in her hand, not unlocking it.

"Good. That's good. The freelance income documentation is what'll matter for the business interruption claim. You lose the studio space, you lose billable months—they need to see that on paper."

"Right." She finally looked at him. "I can rebuild the studio in a rental. Cheaper overhead, honestly. Maybe this is—" She made a vague gesture toward the smoke. "Maybe it's a reset."

"Exactly. You've been wanting to restructure anyway."

She nodded, then turned back to the house. A firefighter was carrying something out the front door—a box, a bin, she couldn't tell. She took three steps toward the tape line before she caught herself.

"Sorry," she said. "I just want to see if—" She stopped.

"What?"

"Nothing. It's stupid." She looked at the bin the firefighter had set on the lawn. Melted plastic on one corner. "There was a box in the hall closet. Just—papers. Old stuff."

Marcus waited.

"My sister sent things back. Years ago. After everything." Delia's voice stayed flat, the way it did when she was working hard to keep it that way. "I kept meaning to go through it. I never—" She exhaled. "Anyway."

"What kind of papers?"

"Letters, I think. I never opened the box." She looked at him. "Which is its own kind of embarrassing, right? Eleven years and I never opened it." She finally unlocked her phone. "Okay. Insurance. Walk me through the business interruption language again."

Marcus did. She typed notes with one hand while her eyes tracked every firefighter who crossed the yard, watching to see what they carried out next.

"I told you, this is the least I can do." Marcus handed him a mug, then kept his hands busy straightening tools he hadn't touched. "You wrote that letter for my sister when nobody else would. Got her the scholarship. I owe you."

Mr. Okafor crouched beside the car. "That was two years ago."

"Debts don't expire." Marcus said it lightly, like a joke, and it almost was. He'd rehearsed the line in the car on the way home, the clean logic of it: someone does something for you, you do something back, the ledger closes. Simple.

But when Mr. Okafor reached past him for the wrench, Marcus didn't flinch. He noticed that he didn't flinch, and then looked away so Mr. Okafor wouldn't notice him noticing.

"Hand me the socket set?"

Marcus found it without being asked twice, which was new, or maybe not new but newly easy. He watched the older man work — the unhurried way he moved, the way he explained each step without making Marcus feel stupid for not already knowing — and felt something in his chest that had nothing to do with owing anyone anything.

"You're a quick learner," Mr. Okafor said.

Marcus almost deflected. Instead he said, "Thanks," and let it land.

They worked for another hour. At some point Marcus stopped tracking the debt — what he'd given, what remained — and just handed over tools when they were needed, asked questions when he had them, laughed once at something that wasn't even that funny. When Mr. Okafor's hand briefly gripped his shoulder to guide him toward the right angle on the bolt, Marcus's whole body went still for a half-second, and then, carefully, didn't.

"Same time next week?" Mr. Okafor asked, packing up.

"I mean — if there's more to show me." Marcus looked at the engine, not at him. "I still owe you a few Saturdays, probably."

Mr. Okafor smiled like he understood something Marcus hadn't said. "Sure. A few Saturdays."

After he left, Marcus stood alone in the garage for a while, both hands wrapped around his mug, not going inside yet.

"What happens after the doctor?" Emmett asked.

"The park." Her foot moved toward the accelerator.

"And after the park?"

She glanced in the mirror again. He was holding the laminated card up, showing it to her, his gap-toothed smile working hard at something—at being brave, she realized. He was practicing being brave by showing her the card, the way she'd shown him: *look at the plan, and the plan will hold you.*

Her foot lifted.

The gap closed. A sedan moved through it, oblivious.

"And after the park," she said, her voice coming out strange and level, "we get hot chocolate. I think I forgot to tell you that part."

Emmett made a sound she hadn't heard from him before—pure, uncomplicated delight. "The card doesn't have hot chocolate."

"I've been sober eleven months," she said. It came out practiced, the way she said it at meetings. "Eleven months and I still don't know what to do with my hands." She held them up as evidence. Dario nodded. He was a good listener. That was why she'd brought him here instead of saying goodbye properly at his car.

Above them, the vaulted ceiling disappeared into shadow. Petra looked up at it, then looked away. She'd been doing that since they arrived — a quick glance, then back to the candle, then up again, a little longer each time, like she was practicing something. The shadows had faces if you stared. She knew they didn't. She was making herself know it.

"The cravings are worst at night," she continued, turning the candle holder over in her hands. "That's when the old logic kicks in. *You could just feel better right now.* You know? The voice that says there's an easier way." She laughed softly. "There isn't. I know there isn't. But it's very convincing at two in the morning."

"What do you do?" Dario asked. "At two in the morning."

"Call someone. Walk. Make tea." She paused. "Come to places like this, apparently."

She looked up again. Longer this time. The ceiling was just stone. A water stain shaped like a hand. She let herself see it as a water stain.

"I think I'm trying to prove I can want things I'm scared of," she said, and then frowned slightly, like she'd surprised herself — like she'd meant to say something else entirely. "The recovery, I mean. Wanting to be well even when it's hard."

Dario didn't point out the shift. He just reached over and held one of her steady hands.

She looked at the ceiling one more time. Held it. Breathed.

The walls were not breathing. She was.

"Right." Mara flipped to a fresh page in her notebook. "And the side door — that's kept unlocked during the service?"

She was writing, but her eyes had drifted to the stained glass above the altar. The blue one. Jonah had called it aggressively mediocre the first time they'd sat here, and she'd laughed so hard a woman in front of them had turned around to stare.

"Detective?"

"The side door. Unlocked." She pulled her gaze back. "I'm going to need a list of every regular congregant. If our thief knew the layout, they've been here before. That's how these things work — familiarity, opportunity." She said it with the practiced confidence of someone who had explained this a hundred times, because she had. "We find who had both, we find our person."

Father Brennan nodded and excused himself to get the membership records.

Mara sat down in the pew.

She told herself it was to review her notes. She opened the notebook, clicked her pen. The wood was smooth and worn under her thighs, the same wood, and she pressed her palm flat against the seat beside her the way you check a stove burner — not to warm your hand, just to confirm the temperature of a thing.

Four months since Jonah had taken the posting in Edinburgh. Not a breakup, they'd both agreed, because they'd never technically been — it wasn't that kind of thing. That had been the whole point of the arrangement. Convenient. Unserious. She'd been the one to suggest it, actually.

Her hand was still on the pew.

Father Brennan returned with a manila folder, and Mara stood quickly, clicking her pen again.

"This is exactly what I need," she said, and meant it. She had a thief to find. She was good at this. She would stand in every room that needed standing in, ask every question that needed asking, follow the evidence wherever it led.

She tucked the folder under her arm and walked toward the exit without looking back at the stained glass.

She looked back at the stained glass.

The base camp chairs were arranged in a horseshoe around the monitor, and Vera found her daughter between takes, hunched over a script with a highlighter. Twenty-two years since she'd last seen Maya in person. She looked like her father.

"I just want to talk," Vera said. "Five minutes."

Maya didn't look up. "You have four."

Vera sat anyway, smoothing her linen slacks. The cancer had taken twelve pounds since spring, and she was grateful for the loose cut. "I'm not here to make amends. I know that ship sailed." She folded her hands in her lap. "I'm here because I'm running out of time and I'd rather spend what's left being honest with someone than performing for hospice volunteers."

Maya's highlighter stopped moving.

"I don't need forgiveness," Vera continued, her voice steady in the way only exhaustion can make a voice steady. "I just need to say things out loud before I can't. That's all I'm asking for."

The PA called a ten-minute hold. Somewhere behind them a generator hummed.

But Vera's eyes had already drifted — not to her daughter's face, not to the hands she hadn't held since Maya was four — but to the open laptop on the folding table nearby. The call sheet visible on screen. *Director: James Foulds.* She recognized the name. Of course she did. She'd been the one to send the emails to the trades, carefully worded, citing *sources close to the production.* She leaned almost imperceptibly forward, scanning the rest of the document, cataloguing who else was attached, which studio, which distributor. Her mouth was still soft with the language of dying, but her fingers had curled around the arm of the chair the way they curled around her phone when she was composing something.

"Mom." Maya's voice was careful. "What did you actually come here to say?"

Vera looked back at her daughter. Her eyes were wet, genuinely. "That I'm sorry I wasn't there. That I know saying it now is almost an insult." She paused. "And that I wanted to see your face once more while I still — " She gestured vaguely at herself.

Maya watched her.

Vera had already noted the production company's logo on the slate board. She would look them up tonight in her hotel room, cross-reference, see who else had worked with Foulds since the story broke. There were two more outlets she hadn't contacted yet.

"I believe you're sick," Maya said finally. "I just don't know why you're here."

Vera reached out and almost touched her daughter's hand. "Neither do I, sweetheart. Neither do I."

Priya leaned over. "I thought you were going to do the blowout again? For the dance?"

Mara's hand moved to the beads before she'd decided to move it. Her fingers closed around them, the smooth amber plastic warm from her skin.

"I don't know," she said. "Maybe."

But she didn't let go.

Her dad was quiet for a second. Then, like he understood something she hadn't quite said out loud: "You don't have to explain it, bug. You just have to decide."

Mara looked at him, then at Priya, then back at her own hand—still holding the beads, knuckles a little white.

"I know," she said. "I already did."

The casino floor hummed its usual Friday-night hymn—slots chiming, chips clicking, the low collective murmur of people feeding something. Marcus stood at the edge of it all, watching Delia count her drawer at Table Six.

"I need you to understand something," he said, stepping closer, lowering his voice to the register he used when he meant business. "This place isn't what it used to be. The people who run it now—they have a philosophy. You either buy in or you don't belong here."

Delia kept counting. "I hear you, Marcus."

"I don't think you do." He leaned against the table's edge. "Sal wants everyone on the floor operating the same way. No more of your little side conversations with the regulars, no more comping drinks on your own call. You do it the way we do it, or I have to let you go. Simple as that."

She looked up. He held her gaze just long enough to make the point land.

But even as he spoke, his eyes kept drifting—past her, toward the main entrance, where the double doors stood propped open to the October air. He'd checked them twice already tonight. He'd also, without quite deciding to, positioned himself twelve feet from the emergency exit, close enough that he could feel the cool draft leaking under it. His jacket was on, which nobody wore on the floor. His car keys were in his front pocket instead of his locker, which wasn't like him.

"The philosophy," Delia said carefully, "or Sal's philosophy?"

"Same thing." He said it firmly. Then he glanced again at the doors.

Three of his best dealers had quit in the past month. The new ownership had installed cameras he didn't recognize in the back hallway. Last week, a man in a gray suit had walked through the counting room without being introduced to anyone, and nobody had explained it afterward. Marcus had started sleeping badly. He'd started keeping his passport in his glove compartment.

"Look," he said, and his voice softened almost against his will, "I'm not asking you to like it. I'm asking you to do it. There's a difference."

Delia studied him for a moment—his jacket, his keys, the way he kept looking at the door.

"Okay, Marcus," she said quietly. "I'll do it your way."

He nodded. Straightened up. Told himself that was the right outcome.

Then he checked the exit one more time.

"Mom." Daniel was already at the counter, waving her over. "I told you, you don't have to be here for this."

"Do you?"

"I do." She tucked her hands into her coat pockets, then seemed to reconsider and unbuttoned it instead, letting the warmth in. "I just think Vermont in February is a strange place to go looking."

"That's the point. Strip everything away. No distractions." He signed the first form. "You think I'm being foolish."

"I think you're being brave," she said, and she meant it, mostly. She was reading the small print on a brochure about home equity loans now, not really absorbing it, just holding something. "I just wonder if you've priced out the heating costs for a cabin rental. In February. In Vermont."

Daniel laughed, a little annoyed. "That's not the point, Mom."

"No," she agreed. She set the brochure down and looked at her son. "What is the point, exactly? In your own words."

He looked at the ceiling, searching. "To figure out who I'd be if nobody was watching. If nothing was expected."

Miriam was quiet. Outside through the glass, sleet had started — she'd noticed it the moment it began, the way the pedestrians outside suddenly hunched and quickened. She watched them for a moment before turning back.

The studio smelled like developer fluid and old wood, and Maren had spent the better part of an hour reorganizing the supply cabinet before her boss, Delia, noticed.

"You don't have to do that," Delia said, leaning in the doorway with two mugs of coffee. She held one out.

Maren looked at the offered mug for a moment before taking it. "I know. I just—I needed something to do with my hands while I think."

"Think about what?"

Maren set the mug on the shelf rather than holding it. "About whether any of this is actually mine, you know? Photography. I picked it up because I needed a skill, and then I got good at it, but I don't know if that means it's *me*." She straightened a row of film canisters that didn't need straightening. "I'm thirty-one. I should know what I'm here for by now."

Delia stepped inside, and Maren—almost imperceptibly—shifted so the cabinet was at her back.

"I think you're a photographer," Delia said simply.

"You have to say that. You pay me."

"I say it because I watched you spend forty minutes last week on a single portrait of a stranger's dog."

Maren almost smiled. She picked up her mug now and wrapped both hands around it. "That dog had interesting eyes."

"Maren."

"I just don't want to invest in something that turns out to be wrong for me." She turned back to the cabinet, rearranging what she'd already arranged. "I've done that before. Committed to things that looked right and weren't."

Delia set her own mug down and sat on the stool across the room—giving the space, though she probably didn't know that's what she was doing. "What would it look like if it *were* right?"

Maren was quiet. Her hands stilled on a box of lens cloths. "I don't know. Maybe it would feel less like waiting for the other shoe."

"That's not really about photography."

"No," Maren admitted, and then caught herself. "But it's about knowing what to give yourself to. What's worth—" She stopped again.

Delia didn't push.

After a moment, Maren picked up her coffee again and actually drank from it this time. Small thing. She glanced at Delia across the room and didn't look away immediately, which was its own kind of accomplishment.

"The Harmon shoot is Thursday," she said finally.

"It is."

"I think I want to try something with natural light. Something less controlled." She paused. "If that's okay."

"It's more than okay." Delia smiled. "It's your call."

Maren nodded, filing that away somewhere careful. *Your call.* She turned back to the cabinet one last time, but this time she left it alone.
